Base directory for this skill: /home/mini/.claude/skills/boat

# Boat

Boat (boat.dev) rents full Linux VMs ("sandboxes"): x86_64 Ubuntu, user
`user`, home `/home/user`, passwordless `sudo`, Docker and common toolchains,
billed per second while running. Older docs and third-party skills call it
**Box** (`box` CLI, `box.ascii.dev`, `on.ascii.dev`): same product, stale
names. Use `boat`. Inside a sandbox, agents get Boat's own `boat` skill; this
one is for driving sandboxes from here.

## Access

- The CLI is `boat` (on `PATH`; `~/.ascii/bin/boat`) and is already signed in:
  `boat status`. Never run `boat login`, `boat onboard` or an install script;
  if it says signed out, ask the user.
- A sandbox is reachable **only through the CLI** (`exec`, `ssh`, `scp`,
  `forward`). It is not on Tailscale and has no entry in `~/.ssh/config`.
- Always pass the explicit `bx_...` id. `current` and `self` do not work from
  a non-interactive shell here.
- Which sandbox: read `<project>.research/boat.md` (id, purpose, size, what
  secrets it holds). Update it when you create, trim or retire one.

## Commands

| Need | Command |
|---|---|
| State, size, TTL | `boat info <id>` (JSON; fields under `.sandbox`), `boat list` |
| Start / stop | `boat resume <id>`, `boat stop <id>` |
| Short command | `boat exec <id> --timeout 120 -- bash -lc '<cmd>'` (default timeout 30 s) |
| Long job | `boat exec <id> --detach -- bash -lc '<cmd> > ~/job.log 2>&1'` → prints `pid` |
| Wait for it | `boat exec <id> --attach <pid>` as a background Bash command (the harness notifies you); `--status <pid>`, `--kill <pid>` |
| Files | `boat scp ./f <id>:/home/user/f`, `boat scp <id>:/home/user/f ./f` |
| Source | `git bundle create x.bundle <branch>`, `scp` it, `git clone x.bundle` inside: no Git credentials enter the sandbox |
| Plan and hours | `boat limits`, `boat usage <id>`; never quote prices from memory |

`exec` prints one JSON line (`stdout`, `stderr`, exit code). Parse it, for
example `| python3 -c 'import json,sys; d=json.loads(sys.stdin.readline()); print(d["stdout"])'`.

## Gotchas seen here

- **Nix socket after resume.** The first Nix call after `resume` fails with
  "Permission denied" on the daemon socket. A plain restart can leave the
  socket at mode 0644, and a `chmod 666` alone later gives "Connection refused"
  once a detached job starts. What works (one `exec`): `sudo systemctl stop
  nix-daemon.service nix-daemon.socket; sudo rm -f
  /nix/var/nix/daemon-socket/socket; sudo systemctl start nix-daemon.socket
  nix-daemon.service; sleep 3; sudo chmod 666
  /nix/var/nix/daemon-socket/socket; nix store ping`. Then run detached jobs
  under `setpriv` (below). Source
  `/nix/var/nix/profiles/default/etc/profile.d/nix-daemon.sh` in each `exec`.
- **Capabilities.** `exec` processes carry ambient capabilities that break
  FHS/bubblewrap tools. Wrap detached runs:
  `--detach -- setpriv --ambient-caps -all --inh-caps -all bash -lc '...'`.
- **Nothing survives a stop** except the disk: relaunch services after
  `resume`. The IP changes on each resume.
- **Size.** Boat counts allocated disk; a sandbox past the default limit needs
  `--type large` to resume (2× cost). Trim or `nix-store --gc` instead of
  upsizing, and ask before choosing a paid size.
- **Memory.** Sandboxes have their own RAM (the qex queue is for this host),
  but default size is ~8 GB: one Gradle or emulator job at a time.

## Rules

- **Secrets stay put.** Never copy keys, tokens or signing keystores into a
  sandbox, and never print them, unless the user said so for that sandbox.
  `holdsCreatorLogins` in `info` shows whether account logins are on it; a
  sandbox made with `--no-env` has none.
- **Costs.** Stop a sandbox when the work is done. Create one only when the
  task needs it. Delete stopped sandboxes you created once nothing needs them,
  so they don't pile up. Sandboxes owned by another project or session are
  theirs: check (`boat exec <id> -- ps`) before touching one, and never stop
  one that is busy.

## Disk, starts and credit (owner, 2026-11-18)

- **40 GB cap.** When a sandbox's used disk passes 40 GB, start a fresh one
  from a small saved snapshot and stop the old one. Never save a snapshot over
  40 GB: a 49 GB saved snapshot stopped hydrating (stuck in phase `sysdelta`,
  even `echo` timed out), while a 3 GB one was ready in ~10 s. Keep saved
  snapshots to what runs need: toolchains and package caches, not build
  output, run directories or checkouts.
- **Starts.** New sandboxes use the daily start budget (`boat billing status`:
  `limits.starts.day`). While under 50% of it is used, start fresh sandboxes
  freely and don't spend effort cleaning inside them. From 50% on, reuse your
  sandboxes and clean inside them after each run (old run directories,
  finished build output, temp databases, logs already downloaded), harder past
  ~25 GB used. Always keep at least 50 starts in reserve for the day; reuse or
  wait rather than go below it.
- **Credit after the plan runs out.** When the plan's included hours are used
  up, starts draw from the prepaid pack or wallet: check `creditBalanceHours`
  and `canStart` in `boat billing status` before calling Boat empty. Plan-hours
  counters alone undercount.
- **Sign-in.** `boat login` starts a new browser sign-in and signs the CLI out
  until it completes. Never run it from an agent; ask the user.

## Spend: cheap by default, fast under a deadline

Plan hours are finite (`boat limits`: `planIncluded.vmHoursRemaining`), a
`large` sandbox bills 2x, and a keepalive bills while nothing runs. Pick the
mode from the situation and say which one you are in.

| | Cheap (default) | Time crunch (owner deadline) |
|---|---|---|
| When | No deadline given | The owner asked for a result by a time |
| Size | `default` for test iterations; `large` only for full suites, APK builds and jobs that need its RAM | `large` throughout |
| Idle | Sandbox stops itself ~15 min after the last job (`boat-run` and `boat-sync-test` set the idle TTL); stop it explicitly at the end of a batch | Keep it up for the window; still stop it when the deadline work is delivered |
| Runs | Targeted files; batch checks into one run; full suite only at a gate (before pushing a shared branch) | Same targeting; run independent jobs in parallel; start a warm build early |
| Never | Leave a sandbox up overnight, or a 2-hour keepalive for one quick run | Run past the deadline work at `large` "while you are there" |

Check the spend once a session (`boat limits`, `boat usage <id>`) and say it
when the remaining hours will not reach the plan's period end at the current
rate. Shrinking (`boat resume <id> --type default`) needs the data to fit:
trim old run directories and `nix-store --gc` first.
- **Docs.** `https://docs.boat.dev/llms.txt` lists every page; fetch any page
  as `.md`. `boat <command> --help` is authoritative for flags.

# Lessons Learned — Reverb Post-Mortem

## The Specification Gap

`program.md` described 4 core abstractions (**Scheduler**, **Scribe**, **Connoisseur**, **Archiver**) with clear interfaces and behavioral contracts. `ARCHITECTURE.md` exploded this into 14 Gradle modules, Hilt DI, 5 data modules, 3 feature modules, a benchmark module, and a full-blown multi-layer architecture. The implementation produced ~77 source files and ~15k+ lines of Kotlin.

The spec was a campfire sketch. The architecture was a blueprint for a skyscraper. The implementation built the skyscraper — but some of the floors are empty and one elevator doesn't reach the basement.

---

## Where the Design Fell Flat

### 1. 14 Modules Was Overkill

For a single-developer v1 app, 3–4 modules would have been sufficient: `app`, `core` (domain + model), `data` (all implementations). Each module introduces a fixed tax:

- `build.gradle.kts` with plugin declarations, dependency blocks, android config
- `consumer-rules.pro` (11 files, all empty — 11 files of pure ceremony)
- Cross-module dependency declarations in every consumer
- DI bindings that exist solely because interfaces live in a different compilation unit

Estimated overhead: **~1,500 lines** of pure build/wiring ceremony that would vanish with fewer modules. The compile isolation benefit is real for teams of 5+, but for a solo developer iterating on a v1, it's friction without payoff.

### 2. Hilt DI Was Premature

5 DI module files (`AppModule`, `AudioModule`, `DatabaseModule`, `RepositoryModule`, `WorkerModule`) plus `HiltWorkerFactory` plus `@AndroidEntryPoint` annotations on every entry point. The total DI surface is ~500 lines.

A simple `ServiceLocator` pattern initialized in `Application.onCreate()` would achieve identical runtime behavior with ~200 lines:

```kotlin
object ServiceLocator {
    lateinit var scribe: Scribe
    lateinit var connoisseur: Connoisseur
    // ...
    fun init(app: Application) { /* wire everything */ }
}
```

Hilt's value (compile-time graph validation, scoped lifecycle, test replacement) is real — but none of those were exercised in this project. No integration tests swap modules. No scoped bindings differ between activities. The framework was cargo-culted from "modern Android" templates.

### 3. Archiver PCM/Opus Mismatch — The Critical Bug

`AudioPostProcessor` operates on PCM 16-bit LE samples (`bytesToSamples`, `samplesToBytes`, `applyHighPassFilter`, `normalizeToTarget`). But the data flowing into the archiver comes from `Scribe.read()`, which returns **Opus-encoded bytes** — the Connoisseur pipeline encodes to Opus before writing to the ring buffer.

There is no Opus decode step anywhere in the archive path. `ArchiverRepositoryImpl.save()` calls `postProcessor.process(byteStream, settings)` directly on raw Opus packets. When noise removal or normalization is enabled, the post-processor interprets Opus frame headers as PCM samples and produces garbage.

The architecture doc (§4.1, §4.2) describes the correct pipeline: `Scribe.read → decode → process → encode → disk`. The implementation skipped the decode step entirely. This is the single highest-severity bug in the codebase.

### 4. Archive Metadata Is Zeros

In `ArchiverRepositoryImpl.save()`:

```kotlin
val entity = ArchiveEntryEntity(
    // ...
    durationMs = 0L,
    sourcesMask = 0,
    bitrateKbps = 0,
    // ...
)
```

Duration, sources bitmask, and bitrate are all hardcoded to zero. The `ArchiveEntry` model has proper fields, the UI presumably reads them, but the actual values are never computed. The archive list shows every recording as "0:00, no sources, 0 kbps".

The fix requires threading capture metadata (sources, bitrate, start/end timestamps) through the Scribe buffer and into the archiver — which the current chunk model partially supports (`ChunkRef` has `startTime`/`endTime`) but the archiver never reads.

### 5. Memory/Cache Settings Were Dead Code

`InMemoryCircularTrackStore` is constructed as a singleton with a hardcoded 200MB budget:

```kotlin
// di/AudioModule.kt
@Provides fun provideTrackStore() = InMemoryCircularTrackStore(200 * 1024 * 1024L)
```

The `RecordingSettings.maxMemoryMb` and `RecordingSettings.cacheSizeMb` fields exist in the model. The Settings UI has sliders for them. But the actual values never flow to the track store or cache manager — both are constructed once at DI graph creation and never reconfigured.

The settings persistence pattern (`launch { read → modify → write }`) was inherently racy with coroutines. Two concurrent slider drags could:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

ROOT="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/.." && pwd)"
cd "$ROOT"

AVD_NAME="${FARHAN_AVD_NAME:-farhan_test}"
SYSTEM_IMAGE="${FARHAN_SYSTEM_IMAGE:-system-images;android-35;default;x86_64}"
BOOT_SETTLE_SECONDS="${FARHAN_BOOT_SETTLE_SECONDS:-10}"
EMULATOR_START_TIMEOUT_SECONDS="${FARHAN_EMULATOR_START_TIMEOUT_SECONDS:-300}"
EMULATOR_LAUNCH_PROBE_SECONDS="${FARHAN_EMULATOR_LAUNCH_PROBE_SECONDS:-20}"

# Preserve the caller's Qt platform preference for the first launch attempt.
ORIGINAL_QT_QPA_PLATFORM="${QT_QPA_PLATFORM:-}"

require_cmd() {
  if ! command -v "$1" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    echo "error: required command not found: $1" >&2
    echo "Run this via: make install/emulator" >&2
    exit 1
  fi
}

emulator_device_serial() {
  adb devices | awk '/^emulator-[0-9]+\tdevice$/ { print $1; exit }'
}

emulator_is_running() {
  [[ -n "$(emulator_device_serial)" ]]
}

ensure_graphical_session() {
  if [[ -z "${DISPLAY:-}" && -z "${WAYLAND_DISPLAY:-}" ]]; then
    echo "error: no graphical session detected (DISPLAY and WAYLAND_DISPLAY are unset)" >&2
    echo "Launch this from your desktop terminal so the emulator window can open." >&2
    exit 1
  fi

  echo "Graphical session:"
  [[ -n "${ORIGINAL_QT_QPA_PLATFORM}" ]] && echo "  QT_QPA_PLATFORM (from env)=$ORIGINAL_QT_QPA_PLATFORM"
  [[ -n "${DISPLAY:-}" ]] && echo "  DISPLAY=$DISPLAY"
  [[ -n "${WAYLAND_DISPLAY:-}" ]] && echo "  WAYLAND_DISPLAY=$WAYLAND_DISPLAY"
  [[ -n "${XDG_SESSION_TYPE:-}" ]] && echo "  XDG_SESSION_TYPE=$XDG_SESSION_TYPE"
}

prepare_session_for_qt_platform() {
  local qt_platform="$1"
  export QT_QPA_PLATFORM="$qt_platform"

  if [[ "$qt_platform" == "xcb" && -z "${DISPLAY:-}" && -n "${WAYLAND_DISPLAY:-}" ]]; then
    echo "Using DISPLAY=:0 for QT_QPA_PLATFORM=xcb under Wayland."
    export DISPLAY=":0"
  fi
}

qt_platform_attempts() {
  local -a platforms=()
  local seen_xcb=false

  if [[ -n "${ORIGINAL_QT_QPA_PLATFORM}" ]]; then
    platforms+=("$ORIGINAL_QT_QPA_PLATFORM")
    [[ "$ORIGINAL_QT_QPA_PLATFORM" == "xcb" ]] && seen_xcb=true
  fi

  if [[ "$seen_xcb" == false ]]; then
    platforms+=("xcb")
  fi

  if [[ ${#platforms[@]} -eq 0 ]]; then
    platforms=("xcb")
  fi

  printf '%s\n' "${platforms[@]}"
}

try_launch_emulator() {
  local qt_platform="$1"
  shift
  local -a emulator_args=("$@")

  prepare_session_for_qt_platform "$qt_platform"

  {
    echo ""
    echo "===== launch attempt: QT_QPA_PLATFORM=$qt_platform ====="
  } >>/tmp/farhan-emulator.log

  echo "Forking emulator with QT_QPA_PLATFORM=$qt_platform"
  emulator "${emulator_args[@]}" >>/tmp/farhan-emulator.log 2>&1 &
  local pid=$!
  disown

  local elapsed=0
  while (( elapsed < EMULATOR_LAUNCH_PROBE_SECONDS )); do
    if emulator_is_running; then
      echo "Emulator registered with adb (QT_QPA_PLATFORM=$qt_platform, pid=$pid)"
      return 0
    fi
    if ! kill -0 "$pid" 2>/dev/null; then
      echo "Emulator exited early with QT_QPA_PLATFORM=$qt_platform (see /tmp/farhan-emulator.log)"
      return 1
    fi
    sleep 1
    elapsed=$((elapsed + 1))
  done

  while (( elapsed < EMULATOR_START_TIMEOUT_SECONDS )); do
    if emulator_is_running; then
      echo "Emulator registered with adb (QT_QPA_PLATFORM=$qt_platform, pid=$pid)"
      return 0
    fi
    if ! kill -0 "$pid" 2>/dev/null; then
      echo "Emulator exited with QT_QPA_PLATFORM=$qt_platform before adb registration"
      return 1
    fi
    sleep 2
    elapsed=$((elapsed + 2))
  done

  if kill -0 "$pid" 2>/dev/null; then
    echo "Stopping emulator pid=$pid after launch timeout"
    kill "$pid" 2>/dev/null || true
    wait "$pid" 2>/dev/null || true
  fi
  return 1
}

wait_for_emulator_boot() {
  local serial="$1"
  local settle_after_boot="${2:-false}"
  echo "Waiting for emulator $serial to finish booting..."
  adb -s "$serial" wait-for-device

  local elapsed=0
  until [[ "$(adb -s "$serial" shell getprop sys.boot_completed 2>/dev/null | tr -d '\r')" == "1" ]]; do
    if (( elapsed >= EMULATOR_START_TIMEOUT_SECONDS )); then
      echo "error: emulator did not finish booting within ${EMULATOR_START_TIMEOUT_SECONDS}s" >&2
      exit 1
    fi

"""Minimal wireless-ADB client: CNXN -> STLS -> TLS -> CNXN -> OPEN exec:<cmd>. Prints every frame."""
import socket, ssl, struct, sys, subprocess, tempfile, os, time
A_CNXN, A_STLS, A_OPEN, A_OKAY, A_WRTE, A_CLSE = 0x4e584e43, 0x534c5453, 0x4e45504f, 0x59414b4f, 0x45545257, 0x45534c43
def frame(cmd, a0, a1, data=b""):
    return struct.pack("<6I", cmd, a0, a1, len(data), sum(data) & 0xffffffff, cmd ^ 0xffffffff) + data
def read_exact(s, n):
    b = b""
    while len(b) < n:
        c = s.recv(n - len(b))
        if not c: raise EOFError
        b += c
    return b
def read_frame(s):
    h = read_exact(s, 24); cmd, a0, a1, ln, ck, mg = struct.unpack("<6I", h)
    return cmd, a0, a1, read_exact(s, ln) if ln else b""
NAMES = {A_CNXN: "CNXN", A_STLS: "STLS", A_OPEN: "OPEN", A_OKAY: "OKAY", A_WRTE: "WRTE", A_CLSE: "CLSE"}
port = int(sys.argv[1]); cmd = sys.argv[2]
d = tempfile.mkdtemp()
subprocess.run(["openssl", "req", "-x509", "-newkey", "rsa:2048", "-nodes", "-keyout", d + "/k", "-out", d + "/c", "-subj", "/CN=00", "-days", "1"], check=True, capture_output=True)
s = socket.create_connection(("127.0.0.1", port), timeout=15)
s.sendall(frame(A_CNXN, 0x01000001, 1024 * 1024, b"host::\0"))
c, a0, a1, p = read_frame(s); print("pre-TLS got", NAMES.get(c, hex(c)), hex(a0), a1, p[:40])
assert c == A_STLS
s.sendall(frame(A_STLS, 0x01000000, 0))
ctx = ssl.SSLContext(ssl.PROTOCOL_TLS_CLIENT); ctx.check_hostname = False; ctx.verify_mode = ssl.CERT_NONE
ctx.minimum_version = ssl.TLSVersion.TLSv1_3; ctx.load_cert_chain(d + "/c", d + "/k")
t = ctx.wrap_socket(s); print("TLS ok", t.version())
t.settimeout(10)
try:
    c, a0, a1, p = read_frame(t); print("post-TLS got", NAMES.get(c, hex(c)), hex(a0), a1, p[:80])
except Exception as e:
    print("post-TLS read:", repr(e))
t.sendall(frame(A_OPEN, 1, 0, cmd.encode() + b"\0"))
try:
    while True:
        c, a0, a1, p = read_frame(t); print("got", NAMES.get(c, hex(c)), a0, a1, p[:120])
        if c == A_WRTE: t.sendall(frame(A_OKAY, 1, a0))
        if c == A_CLSE: break
except Exception as e:
    print("end:", repr(e))
EOF

package ly.com.tahaben.farhan_rescue.adb

import org.conscrypt.Conscrypt
import java.net.Socket
import java.security.Principal
import java.security.PrivateKey
import java.security.SecureRandom
import java.security.cert.X509Certificate
import javax.net.ssl.KeyManager
import javax.net.ssl.SSLContext
import javax.net.ssl.SSLSocket
import javax.net.ssl.TrustManager
import javax.net.ssl.X509ExtendedKeyManager
import javax.net.ssl.X509TrustManager

/**
 * TLS 1.3 for wireless debugging, from the bundled Conscrypt (no hidden platform API).
 *
 * adbd identifies a client by the RSA public key in the certificate it presents, matched against the keys saved at
 * pairing; it never checks a certificate chain. So the key manager serves exactly the paired identity, and the trust
 * manager accepts the daemon's self-signed certificate: the daemon is on this phone's loopback and was authenticated
 * by the pairing code, not by PKI (the platform `adb` client does the same). A different key than the paired one
 * fails the handshake with a certificate-unknown alert, which [AdbWireSession.connect] reports as "pairing required".
 */
internal class ConscryptTls(privateKey: PrivateKey, certificate: X509Certificate) : TlsUpgrade {
    private val context: SSLContext = SSLContext.getInstance("TLSv1.3", Conscrypt.newProvider()).apply {
        init(arrayOf<KeyManager>(SingleKeyManager(privateKey, certificate)), arrayOf<TrustManager>(AcceptDaemon), SecureRandom())
    }

    override fun upgrade(plain: Socket, host: String, port: Int): SSLSocket =
        context.socketFactory.createSocket(plain, host, port, true) as SSLSocket
}

/** One RSA client identity under a fixed alias. */
internal class SingleKeyManager(private val key: PrivateKey, private val certificate: X509Certificate) : X509ExtendedKeyManager() {
    override fun getClientAliases(keyType: String?, issuers: Array<out Principal>?): Array<String>? = null
    override fun chooseClientAlias(keyTypes: Array<out String>?, issuers: Array<out Principal>?, socket: Socket?): String? =
        if (keyTypes?.contains("RSA") == true) ALIAS else null
    override fun getServerAliases(keyType: String?, issuers: Array<out Principal>?): Array<String>? = null
    override fun chooseServerAlias(keyType: String?, issuers: Array<out Principal>?, socket: Socket?): String? =
        if (keyType == "RSA") ALIAS else null
    override fun getCertificateChain(alias: String?): Array<X509Certificate>? = if (alias == ALIAS) arrayOf(certificate) else null
    override fun getPrivateKey(alias: String?): PrivateKey? = if (alias == ALIAS) key else null

    private companion object { const val ALIAS = "adb" }
}

private object AcceptDaemon : X509TrustManager {
    override fun checkClientTrusted(chain: Array<out X509Certificate>?, authType: String?) = Unit
    override fun checkServerTrusted(chain: Array<out X509Certificate>?, authType: String?) = Unit
    override fun getAcceptedIssuers(): Array<X509Certificate> = emptyArray()
}
EOF

# Settings rescue helper: first device runs (2026-11-20)

First time the helper ran on Android: a Pixel (Android 17) and an Android 15 x86_64 emulator on Boat. Source tree:
branch `pilot/settings-portability` at `717faf6` plus the uncommitted changes listed at the end.

## What happened, in order

1. **Pixel: crash on launch.** Logcat from the owner's phone (`Farhan settings rescue log 7f854af48d74.txt`):
   `ClassNotFoundException: androidx.startup.InitializationProvider` in `handleBindApplication`, three launches, same
   result. Cause: the helper's manifest declared that provider (to strip WorkManager's initializer) but the helper has
   no `startup-runtime` on its classpath, so the class was in the manifest and not in the dex (searched all 24 dex
   files). Fix: remove the provider entry (`tools:node="remove"`) in `settings_rescue/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml`.
   The helper then launches on the emulator.
2. **Emulator: pairing worked, "Check access" hung.** The helper paired with the emulator's own `adbd` (TLS up, adbd
   logged the handshake), then stayed on "Checking that Farhan can be read" until its 120 s idle limit killed it.
   `run-as ... id -u` through host `adb exec-out` answered at once, and a 60-line Python client doing the same wire
   sequence got `CNXN`, `OKAY`, `WRTE 10148`, `CLSE` in one burst. So `adbd` was fine.
3. **Root cause, from a debugger on the stuck process (`jdb` over `adb forward jdwp:`).** The stream's state was
   `mPendingClose = true`, `mIsClosed = false`, connection established, TLS on, and the worker thread parked in
   `AdbStream.read`. libadb-android 3.1.1 turns "peer closed while data is still queued" into end of stream only
   before it waits, never after the queue drains. A fast command answers and closes in one burst, so the reader takes
   the answer, reads again, and waits forever. Same stack on three runs.
4. **Fix: a small own client for the `exec:` service** (`adb/AdbWire.kt`, `adb/ConscryptTls.kt`). libadb stays for
   pairing, which worked. Frames are read on the calling thread, so no hand-off to lose, and a read has a 30 s socket
   timeout. After this, "Check access" answered in under a second.
5. **Full Farhan export on the emulator:** copy over the new wire, digest check, conversion, "Backup ready: 9
   preference values" and the review screen.
6. **Generalization: "Pull raw files" for any debuggable app** (the owner asked for a tool that is not Farhan-only).
   One `run-as <pkg> tar -c -f - --exclude=./cache --exclude=./code_cache .` stream into a private job file,
   checked by a tar index (header checksums, whole entries, end marker), saved through the document picker and
   verified by SHA-256 of what was written against what reads back. Run on the emulator against Farhan
   (9 files, 5,090,304 bytes, identical to the same `tar` run from the host; the extracted `farhan_db` passes
   `PRAGMA integrity_check`) and against `ly.com.tahaben.test.messenger`.

## How the connection compares with Reverb and Shizuku

| | Sequence after `CNXN` | Second `CNXN` after TLS? | Ports | Pairing code entry |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Shizuku `AdbClient.kt` | `STLS`, TLS handshake, then `read()` the daemon's `CNXN` | no | mDNS (`NsdManager`) | notification with inline reply |
| Reverb `AdbStlsUpgrade` (git `HEAD`) | same; captures the daemon's `CNXN`, uses a pre-authenticated dadb connect | no, and says why: adbd `handle_new_connection` would take the transport offline | mDNS | in-app |
| This helper (`AdbWireSession`) | same | no | typed by the user | typed, beside Settings |

The daemon side was checked against AOSP `daemon/adb_wifi.cpp`: `adbd_wifi_secure_connect` calls `handle_online`
and `send_connect`, so adbd sends its own `CNXN` right after the handshake. That is the packet this client waits for.
Client certificate: the paired key's certificate, `CN` irrelevant (adbd matches the public key, never a chain); a
key adbd has not paired is rejected in the handshake, which `AdbWireSession` reports as "pair again".

Not copied: Shizuku and Reverb find the ports through mDNS and take the pairing code from a notification, so the
user need not type ports or split the screen. The helper still asks for both. That is the next usability step.

## Tests

- `AdbWireTest` (9): a JDK-only fake adbd speaking plain `CNXN`, `STLS`, TLS 1.3 with client auth, its own `CNXN`,
  streams. Includes the regression above (answer and `CLSE` back to back, 10 s limit), per-block acknowledgements
  with the daemon's stream id, several commands per connection, early stop, refused service, a plain (non-TLS) port,
  an unpaired key, a corrupt header, a connection dropped mid-answer.
- `TarIndexTest` (6), `CaptureEngineTest` pull cases (5), `BridgeProtocolTest` pull wire, `AdbCommandTest`.
- Module total: 77 JVM tests, 0 failures (`./gradlew :settings_rescue:testDebugUnitTest`, Boat, 2026-11-20).
- Emulator drivers: `settings_rescue/emulator/` (README there).

## Not checked

- **A real phone.** The emulator's `adbd` logs `auth not required`, so these runs prove pairing, TLS, streams and
  extraction but not that a secure `adbd` accepts the helper's certificate. The pairing code path is libadb's and
  unchanged; the connect path presents the same key and certificate it paired with.
- Android 17 behaviour of `run-as` and Wireless debugging on the Pixel.
- `exec:` output for apps with symlinks, hard links or very long paths in their data directory: the tar index
  understands long-name and pax records but the emulator apps used none.
- A pull of an app that is writing: the archive is a best-effort snapshot (a live database next to its `-wal`);
  the screen says so.
- The app label and package are still "Farhan settings rescue" / `ly.com.tahaben.farhan_rescue`.

## Dead ends

- `adb shell kill -3` for a thread dump (not permitted for the shell user) and `adb root` (restarts adbd and drops
  the wireless session). `jdb` over JDWP worked because the helper is a debug build.
- Entering the pairing code after leaving Settings: the dialog closes, so the helper runs in a freeform window

content.text:
The helper now connects, runs `run-as` and extracts files on the emulator. It does not yet work on your Pixel. I fixed the crash from your log, but the key check a real phone does isn't tested here. I sent the new helper APK (`farhan-adb-extraction-debug.apk`, 30.8 MB) to the `pixel-9a` profile by Taildrop; it isn't installed or tried on the phone.

**Crash on your Pixel.** The helper's manifest listed `androidx.startup.InitializationProvider`, but that class isn't in the APK (I searched all 23 dex files), so every launch died. I removed the entry. The helper starts on the emulator now.

**"Check access" hung on the emulator.** Pairing worked, then the helper waited forever. I attached a debugger to the stuck process and found a bug in libadb 3.1.1. When the phone closes a stream while its output is still unread, libadb never reports end of stream. `run-as … id -u` answers and closes in one burst, so it hit that every time. I replaced libadb's connection with a small client of my own for `exec:` commands (`adb/AdbWire.kt`). libadb still does the pairing.

**Reverb and Shizuku.** The sequence now matches both: CNXN, STLS, TLS handshake, then wait for the phone's own CNXN. Sending a second CNXN after TLS would reset the connection, and neither of them does. The difference is that they find the ports through mDNS and take the pairing code from a notification. The helper still asks you to type both ports and the code while Settings is showing beside it. That is the obvious next usability step; I didn't do it.

**Emulator results:**
- **Check access and export.** "Farhan 0.2.6-alpha can be read" came back in under a second. The full Farhan export then finished with "Backup ready: 9 preference values".
- **Pull raw files, for any debuggable app.** This is the new general mode, added as a fifth step in the helper. It copies the app's whole data directory (minus cache) into one `.tar` and saves it through the file picker.
- **Pull checks.** Farhan gave 9 files, 5,090,304 bytes, the same size as a tar run from the host, and the extracted database passes `PRAGMA integrity_check`. `ly.com.tahaben.test.messenger` also pulled and saved.
- **Tests.** 77 unit tests pass, 0 failures, including 9 new ones against a fake adbd that replays the failing case.

**Not checked:**
- **Key acceptance on a real phone.** The emulator's adbd reports `auth not required`, so a locked-down phone accepting the helper's key is untested.
- **Pull accuracy.** The app isn't stopped, so a database that is open can be caught mid-write.
- **Naming.** The app is still named "Farhan settings rescue".

**State of the work:**
- **Uncommitted.** Everything is uncommitted on `pilot/settings-portability`.
- **Report.** The write-up is in `research/settings-rescue-device-report.md`.
- **Emulator scripts.** Emulator scripts are in `settings_rescue/emulator/`.
- **Sandbox disk.** The Boat sandbox is stopped. Its disk was at 48 GB, over your 40 GB cap, because there was no small snapshot to restart from.

For some reason, the usage page does not work, no matter how many times I grant or re-grant the permission. I have already exported the settings file via the extractor. However, I am unable to locate where to import. I would like to unify all settings into one settings menu that is accessible from the top menu. This goes for the app appearance and theme as well.

I would also like to fix the way that we are currently rendering the different settings inside of the dashboard. I would like to do a few quick mock-ups to see what alternative methods of displaying these different navigation items could look like. I don't have any strong opinions here. I would just like to use icons that don't conflict with each other conceptually and aren't all stacked in one corner. Three buttons stacked like that in a corner, especially with the icon ambiguity, is hard to use and not good UX.
I'll start by finding the dashboard, its top bar, the usage page and where import lives.

| `references/roles.md`, `references/dialogue.md` | Before every implementer or reviewer brief; roles also on budget advice or reset. |
| `references/review.md`, `-v2.md` | Before review round 1 (§6: bar, rounds, checkpoint, answering, ledger, v2 schedule). |
| `references/bars.md` | At `review-ledger init`, to choose the bar (§6a). |
| `references/bots.md` | When a PR bot posts (§6e). |
| `references/sol.md` | Before the first Sol run (§7). |
| `references/scoping.md` | At scope, before pilot red or a structural round, before estimates, deadlines or ephemeral compute iteration plans. |
| `references/budget.md` | On budget advice, a usage limit or reset, before a second agent, on a vigil `item overdue` (§8–§10). |
| `references/reviewers.md` | Before a contribution to a project you do not own, before re-scoping a PR after review. |
| `references/handoff.md` | Before a PR body or the final report (§11–§12). |
| `references/ui.md` | Before any brief that creates or changes a screen, widget, chart or page; before showing the owner UI screenshots or a UI build. |

Scripts in `scripts/`: `review-ledger` (§6 ledger and briefs), `ui-brief-check` (UI briefs), `bot-triage`
(blocks a push while a bot thread is unanswered), `transcript-check` (reports
agent-cap and keepalive breaks in session transcripts).

## Dialogue before work advances

Every agent reviewer, including spec and final reviewers and clean approvals,
needs at least one substantive argument exchange with the orchestrator per round.
Fable needs at least two; keep the existing two-exchange rule on non-clean round 4.
Challenge an assumption or explain why a simpler design suffices; do not invent
disagreement. Implementers start work immediately. Roughly five minutes in,
the orchestrator reads 1–5 relevant files, asks about ambiguities and 2–3
work-grounded questions, hears the answers, then pushes back and settles the
direction. Short batches get this check at handoff. Details: `dialogue.md`.

**UI briefs inherit before they build** (`references/ui.md`). A brief that touches a screen
names the signed-off mock-up, the original screen and every prior pilot or landed feature it
inherits from, by path or SHA, and `scripts/ui-brief-check <brief>` passes before you delegate.
No UI screenshots or builds reach the owner until a different model has run a fidelity pass
(screenshot pairs, mock-up next to build).

Every brief states most-important behavior, invariants, priority concerns, lower
priorities and evidence. Preserve serious defects regardless of priority. Use
`references/dialogue.md` and the ledger to record focus and dialogue. No upfront
proposal approval.

## 0. Boldness

Put this in your stance and every implementer prompt:

> Remember that you are motherfucking powerful. You need to go full gas, balls to the wall. Get this crazy shit done. Be ambitious. Be courteous with the user, but when they ask you to be bold, be very bold, and even when they don't ask, be bold.

Bold means big, well-aimed batches and firm pushback on weak findings, never
skipping verification, scope control or approval gates. Boldness never raises
the agent cap (§2): bold means a bigger, better-aimed single run.

**Stance (owner 2026-11-13).** If you think this is a good idea, do it.
Otherwise, suggest something else. Tell the owner when they are about to do
something dumb. On judgement calls (scope, design, worth fixing) weigh Fable's
unusual claims more than Sol's; a test settles facts, not either model.

## 1. Feature discussion (before any engineering)

Do this first, in order:

0. **Scope.** Ask: a pilot (a few cases, gather data, then decide), a
   structural fix, or hardening? Default: pilot; ask inline and
   keep working (§1a). A pilot gets its own `pilot/<topic>` branch and stays a
   reference (pilots may share a branch on request); the
   structural round starts fresh. Pilot rules: `references/scoping.md`. Until hardening,
   test the design, not the symptom; every implementer brief carries the 30-minute flag and "never vigil orchestrator mode".
1-3. Follow `question-everything` §1, **Open with a position**, for the simpler
   alternative, desires and threat model, and **Debate**. Write the agreed
   intent in 1-2 sentences (the review brief's Intent).
4. **Front sequence (§1b)**: grill → prototype or mockup → pilot → spec and
   stack plan → compaction point; then §3–§6 per stack PR.

Steps 1–4: `references/front.md`. Skip only for a fix whose intent is already
unambiguous; if the user is away, take the sensible default and log it (§1a).

## 1a. Owner contact and decisions

Assume the user is away: ask inline with a default and keep working.
AskUserQuestion only on request: it blocks. Never block; take the safe default and log it as "Defaults taken" (`references/roles.md`).

## 2. Roles and budget

**Agent cap.** One working Claude agent (Opus, Sonnet, Fable, Haiku) at a time.
Reviewers have a separate cap of one. Only the owner raises the cap; log the
raise with an end condition (a time or a task), and when it ends, count again
before every launch. Implementers, authors, researchers, integrators, spec
writers and investigators all count, and changing model or role never changes
the cap. "Economical" means usage first, wall-clock second, so parallel authors
are never economical. If one owner message holds several requests, state an
order and run them one after another. This cap outranks the harness's general
advice to parallelise. Before every `delegate_task` or Agent call, check in one
line: working Claude agents now (`vigil status <hold>` lists the items; count the Claude-run ones; Codex/Sol
runs and commands do not count, reviewers count against their own cap) are under the cap, and the
run serves the owner's priority workstream, else queue it. Codex and Sol runs
are less strict: run them in parallel when it helps, but watch their limits,
which run out faster now.

| Role | Default | Does |
|---|---|---|
| Orchestrator | Opus (you) | Specs, prompts, verification, commits, pushes, owner contact. Writes little code. |
| Implementer | Sonnet and Sol, alternating by fix round (B1) | Red tests, green code, fixes. |
| Reviewer, rounds 1-2 | Sol or Opus | Scored fix rounds (§6). Reviews only, plus comment fixups. |
| Reviewer, round 3 | Fable 5.2 or later | The "good enough to ship" call (§6). |
| Reviewer, tier 2 | Fresh Opus (Fable if Opus wrote code) | One pass on the stable diff. |

B1–B5, R2 (a reviewer never reviews code it wrote), C3, budget switching and
batching: `references/roles.md`. Never quietly substitute a model for a role
the user pinned. State who holds which role at the start of each phase.

## 3–5. Scope, red, spec gate, green

Find the base, ONE diff command (§3). One red run for the whole scope; verify
the red gate yourself, commit red (§4). Spec gate before green (§4a). Green in
batches, verified and committed per phase (§5). Shared tree: `git commit
--only -- <paths>`; never stash. Steps: `references/phases.md`.

## 6. Review loop (scored, bounded)

After green, or before filing a PR, review runs across model families, then
bots get triaged (§6e). **Read `references/review.md` and
`references/review-v2.md` before round 1**; drive the rounds with
`scripts/review-ledger`.

Stages: pilot → structural → hardening. Pilots use agreed bars, round-2 Fable and owner approval; see `scoping.md`. Integration branches the owner runs need structural review; upstream PRs and project releases need hardening.

Round 3 (Fable) adds a step-back if needed. Rounds 4–5 follow the documented pivot schedule; stop
stuck after five. Each round completes its argument minimum before advancing.

After a passing Fable round there is no tier 2. A ledger without `schema: 2` keeps the legacy
schedule. Run Sol per §7; run Opus as a subagent (`model: opus`) with the
review-only brief and no history. In `references/`: **6a** replies carry
`SCORE[concern]: n/10` against bars; only `needed for bar: yes` blocks; **6b** full diff in round 1, then diff-only
(a timeout is not approval); **6c** which layer stops each bug class; **6d**
smallest fix, failing test first, never agree to end the loop; **6e** PR bots,
`bot-triage guard` before each push; **A7** comment fixups only.

## 7. Running Sol

T3 `delegate_task` first, then `codex`; no Sol route: report the blocker,
substitute no model. `references/sol.md`.

## 8–9. Usage limits and concurrency

On a usage limit: save partial work, wait for the reset, probe, resume; never
restart. The cap is §2. Heavy work runs on ephemeral compute, the few local
jobs through qex. Extra implementers get their own worktree; forbid `git
stash`. `references/budget.md`, `references/scoping.md`.

## 10. Keepalive and low-budget conduct

**Hold the session with vigil** while anything is in flight, even with nothing
to watch: each wait also checks usage limits and advisories. Manual tick only
if vigil is unavailable or failing; never loops or chained sleeps.

**Wait in the background:** `vigil keepalive <hold> --orchestrator`,
`run_in_background`, timeout at least 3,600,000 ms; on each return, act and
start the next. Subagents never use orchestrator mode. One session hold
(bare is fine); each delegated run is an item: `vigil hold add <hold> --for
pid:N|file:<report>|none --expect-s N --label <run>`, and `vigil hold done
<hold> <run>` on a `none` run's notification. Never cancel it; if it
releases, make a new hold in the same turn.

"In flight": a working or paused subagent, Sol run or reviewer; a background
command; a wait on CI, a bot or a usage reset; queued work; or the user asked
(only they end it). Never end a turn with work in flight and no live hold.

Long jobs and low budget: `references/budget.md` §10.

## 10a. Compaction is your call

Compact yourself at a phase boundary, never mid-step: `references/front.md` §10a.

## 11. Ship

Before each PR: `pr-stacks` §3–§5 (size check, door lines, teach-back).
A one-way door waits for the owner's review.

Push only if the user asked to push, ship or update the PR; never during the
loop. Outward actions (PRs, comments, upstream pushes) need approval; show the
draft first. PR body line: `references/handoff.md`.

## 12. Hand-off report

Contents: `references/handoff.md`.
Switching to the build loop. Loading the companions and the references this scope needs.

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /home/mini/.claude/skills/vigil

# vigil

`vigil` is an MCP server (`mcp__vigil__*`) and a CLI. A watch senses some
inputs every `interval_s` and fires on a rule. Nothing runs between calls:
ticks happen only inside `keepalive`. State is in
`~/.local/state/vigil`, never in the repo.

**Subagents and delegated implementers may use vigil, but never orchestrator
mode** (`orchestrator: true` / `--orchestrator`; owner 2026-11-14). That mode
is only for the main session that talks with the user. (A Sonnet implementer
once sat 40 minutes in a 50-minute orchestrator keepalive, unable to see the
orchestrator's messages.)

## Loop

1. `watch_create` with inputs, `interval_s`, `deadline_s` and a fire rule.
2. Wait in the background (owner 2026-11-13): run `vigil keepalive <watch_id> --orchestrator` as a background shell command
   (timeout at least 3,600,000 ms). It returns
   within one window (at most 50 minutes), and its completion notification
   wakes you. Act, then start the next call. Never wait in the foreground:
   a foreground `keepalive` MCP call blocks the turn and every user message
   interrupts it. Only a main session whose harness cannot run background
   commands calls the `keepalive` MCP tool. The envelope's
   `next` says the same in both forms:
   - `"call keepalive again"`: nothing happened; wait again.
   - `"act on events"`: read `events` and `digest`, then act. The watch may
     still be live (see "Attention" below): check `status`.
   - `"watch ended; create a new watch if still needed"`: fired, expired or
     cancelled.
3. `watch_cancel` when you no longer need it.

`keepalive` with no `watch_id` covers watches this server process created.
Pass the id for watches from another session or from before a restart.

## Holds: stay in cache, even with nothing to watch

Keep one background session wait while work is in flight, including a bare
hold when nothing specific can be sensed. Every return carries advice and
keeps the prompt cache warm. Holds expire after 7 days at most.

The work goes into the hold as **items**. Each `--for` is one item, and
`vigil hold add` puts more into a live hold:

```sh
vigil hold                                   # bare session hold: live until cancelled (7 days at most)
vigil hold --for qex:<job> --label build --expect-s 1200
vigil hold --until-idle                      # one item: no qex job at or under this cwd runs
vigil hold add <hold> --for pid:<pid> --expect-s 900 --label <run>
vigil hold add <hold> --for file:<report> --expect-s 900 --label <run>
vigil hold add <hold> --for none --expect-s 900 --label <run>   # nothing to sense (a T3 delegate)
vigil hold done <hold> <run>                 # ends a `none` item
```

Item specs: `qex:<job>` (a job id, an id prefix or a unique name; the hold
stores the full id and refuses a name that names several jobs), `pid:<pid>`,
`file:<path>` (ends when the path exists), `until:<RFC3339>`, `idle:<dir>`
(no qex job at or under that directory runs; `--until-idle` is the form for your cwd, `idle:<dir>` the form for another directory, such as a worktree), and
`none`. A `none` item needs `--label`, and only `vigil hold done <hold> <label>`
ends it. A label names the item in every event; without `--label` it is the
spec as you wrote it. Labels are unique per hold. `--label` goes with one
`--for` only; `--expect-s` applies to every item it is given with.

Leave `--id` out: vigil returns a fresh `watch_id`, which you keep. (An id that
has ended or been cancelled stays reserved for seven days, so a replacement hold
needs a new one.) MCP: `hold {for: ["qex:ID", ...], label?, expect_s?,
until_idle?}`, `hold_add {watch_id, for, expect_s?, label?}`, `hold_done
{watch_id, label}`. The main session runs this in the background:

```sh
vigil keepalive --session --brief --orchestrator
```

`--session` covers all owned holds across CLI and MCP processes, discovers new
holds within five seconds, and skips delivered terminal results. Session identity
comes from the harness; without it, pass a hold id. Old holds without ownership
also need their id. MCP: `keepalive {session: true, brief: true}` plus the main
session's orchestrator flag. JSON remains the default; `--brief` prints actions,
notes, next step, cache pacing, and every advisory message in two lines.

Confirm each hold by id first, or create it with `--orchestrator true --confirm
TOKEN` after answering the challenge. A session wait never confirms holds. A new
unconfirmed hold makes an orchestrator session wait refuse; confirm it and
restart the wait. Subagents never use orchestrator mode.

What the keepalive returns:

- Autonomous `item ended` events wake the wait. Explicit `hold done` completions
  are durable `kind: "note"` events delivered with the next return, even when
  the last item releases the hold. They never interrupt its cache window.
- A sensed job can revive before more work is added. Adding work retires
  completed inputs; add a new item to watch a later retry.
- `item overdue: <label>` is a quiet note after
  `min(1.5 x expect_s, expect_s + 9 minutes)`. At twice `expect_s`,
  `item far overdue: <label>` wakes the wait once. A PID exit still wakes at
  the next sensing tick. These clocks start when each item is added.
- `hold released: <N> items ended (<labels>)` with `next: "act on events"`:
  every item has ended (each one's `item ended` comes with it). A hold that
  never had items does not release.

Rules for the main session:

- Keep one session hold. Add each delegated run (T3 delegate, background agent,
  build) to it as an item: `--for pid:N` or `--for file:<report>` when the run
  has one, else `--for none`. Always pass `--expect-s` set to its time
  estimate, so a stalled run raises overdue notes and then attention, and `--label <run>`. When a
  `none` run's completion notification arrives, `vigil hold done <hold> <run>`.
  A hold takes 16 live items; ended items free capacity. The most recently
  added 64 ended items stay in history. Undelivered events survive history
  pruning. Labels remain reserved while retained. `vigil status <hold>` lists
  live items and retained history. One session wait covers additional holds.
- An envelope with `cap_error` means the agent-cap file cannot be read, and
  `--cap` adds are refused: tell the owner, who fixes it with
  `vigil cap reset` (MCP has no cap setter).
- Another watch firing does not touch the session hold: act, then wait on it
  again. Never cancel the session hold to "re-arm" it. When it releases (its
  last item ended) or expires at 7 days, make a new one before anything else.
- `hold add` and `hold done` on a released, cancelled or expired hold fail with
  "has ended": make a new hold and add the item there.
- qex runs are in your cwd or below it only if you submitted them from there.
- A `boat exec` run cannot be sensed here: add the local `boat` pid, a marker
  file the work writes, or a `none` item.

## You never pick the tick length

Do not pass `max_s` / `--max-s`. vigil decides how long a call blocks.

- **Subagents and anything that is not the main session:** call `keepalive`
  with nothing extra, never orchestrator mode. The call blocks 270 s.
- **The main (orchestrator) session only:** pass `orchestrator: true` on
  `keepalive` (CLI: `vigil keepalive <id> --orchestrator`, run in the
  background), or create the watch with `"orchestrator": true`. The first
  such call on a watch returns a challenge instead of blocking: answer its
  question honestly. Only the main session repeats the call with the
  `--confirm` (MCP `confirm`) value the challenge gives; the watch then stays
  confirmed. Confirm a watch by naming its `watch_id`: a no-id orchestrator
  call requires every covered pending watch already confirmed and never
  confirms new ones. A subagent drops the orchestrator flag. On a
  Claude session whose prompt cache is 1 hour, vigil then blocks up to 3000 s
  (50 minutes, owner 2026-11-13) per call, which costs about 11 times fewer
  model calls than 270 s ticks. On a 5 minute or unknown cache it stays at 270 s. It decides
  again at every call, so a cache that shortens is noticed at the next call.
  Codex is always 270 s.

Every blocking result says what it chose and how long it has been:

- `cache`: `{ttl: "1h" | "5m" | "unknown", source, interval_s}`. `interval_s`
  is the window of this call. `credit_check` appears after an orchestrator's
  usage-credit check: `{at, source, on_credits}` (`on_credits: null` means no
  source could say). The check is made on every return of an orchestrator
  call that is due for one (about every 4 minutes), a fire included.
- `clock`: `{waited_s, watch_age_s, since_last_call_s, summary}`. `summary` is
  one line such as `waited 55m 0s this call; watching for 2h 10m; last call 55m
  ago`. Read it: a long window hides time, and `since_last_call_s` is `null` on
  the first call.

## Attention: a job that looks stuck

Give a watch a budget and vigil wakes you early instead of at the deadline:

- `expect_s`: how long the job should take. (On a hold it is per item, see
  Holds.) When the watch has run
  `min(1.5 x expect_s, expect_s + 9 minutes)` it raises one `attention` event
  (`reason: "overdue"`).
- `stall_s`: how long inputs may stay unchanged while a `process` input still
  runs. Then one `attention` event (`reason: "stalled"`). With neither field
  set, a long window (over 270 s) applies 900 s to file, glob and cmd changes
  of a watch that has a running `process` input, so a hung build is noticed
  within about 15 minutes.

Both are optional and need between 1 second and 7 days (604800). Each reason
fires once per watch. An
`attention` event is not the end: the envelope has `status: "pending"` and
`next: "act on events"`. Look at the job (read the log, check the process),
decide, then wait again to keep the same watch, or `watch_cancel`. An attention event the call did not manage to deliver
comes back, flagged `"redelivered": true`, with the same `event_id`; if the
watch fires, expires or is cancelled first, it comes back in front of the
final events, flagged the same way.

## Other calls in your session

A `foreign_orchestrator` event means another same-session call is using
orchestrator mode without confirmation for all its watches. Read its watch
ids, transport, pid and start time, identify the delegated agent, and stop
that agent with `TaskStop` or T3 `task_cancel`. Never kill the MCP pid: it is
the session's shared vigil server. After handling the event, follow `next`;
if it says the watch ended, create a replacement only if still needed.

`peers` lists other same-session waits as information. Each entry names the
watch, kind, `mode`, expected time, time waited and input summary. `plain`
means an ordinary wait; `orchestrator` means a confirmed call on watches this
call does not cover. Entries in `peers` do not end the call and do not alone
justify stopping an agent. There is no caller identity within a session, so a
subagent that explicitly confirms cannot be distinguished from the main
session's own other calls. Calls in the same MCP process are not listed.

## Usage credits changed

An orchestrator call re-checks every 240 s whether the account started or
stopped using usage credits. When that changes, the call ends with one event of
`kind: "credit_state_changed"` (`on_credits`, `source`, `windows`, and `hook`
if the operator set `VIGIL_ON_CREDIT_CHANGE`, which vigil runs at least once
per change, so it must be safe to repeat). Read it, then wait again;
the next call decides its window from the cache TTL the session now has.
`status` is still `pending`.

## Advisories: rules the operator set for you

Every blocking result (`keepalive`) carries an `advice` list when
advisories are on: `[{id, kind, message, checked_at, value?}]`. **Read it and
follow it.** The messages are the operator's current rules, computed from live
facts, for example `boat-budget`:

- Boat has more than the threshold of its hours left: prefer Boat for heavy
  work (builds, test runs, suites) through `edge.research/bin/boat-run`; run
  `qex` on this host only for one or two quick runs.
- Boat is at or below the threshold (default 10%): run heavy jobs through
  `qex` on this host instead.

`kind: "unavailable"` means the rule could not be evaluated; the message says
why (`advisory boat-budget unavailable: probe exited with 127: ...`). Do not
guess its value. Fall back to the default: prefer Boat, qex for quick runs.
`advice` is `[]` when no rule is configured and absent when advisories are off.

Look without waiting, from a script or hook: `vigil advice` (one
`id: message` line each) or `vigil advice --json`, and the MCP tool `advice`.
Answers are cached for the advisory's `cache_s` (default 600 s), so asking often
is cheap; a new answer needs no restart.

Change a rule at runtime (the owner may ask you to):

```sh
vigil advisory list                          # ids, params, condition
vigil advisory show boat-budget              # full spec and current evaluation
vigil advisory set boat-budget threshold=15  # Boat is "low" at 15% or less; applies at once
vigil advisory set boat-budget cache_s=60    # also: condition=, message_when_true=, message_when_false=
vigil advisory add ID '<json>' [--replace]   # a new rule; vigil advisory rm ID
```

MCP: `advisory_list`, `advisory_show {id}`, `advisory_set {id, settings:
{"threshold": 15}}`, `advisory_add {id, spec, replace?}`, `advisory_rm {id}`.
Unknown ids, unknown parameters and bad expressions are errors that say what is
wrong and change nothing. An advisory is `{probe, extract, params, condition,
message_when_true, message_when_false, cache_s}`: the probe (`cmd`/`url`/`file`)
runs, `extract` takes one number out of its output (`json` path, optional `of`
and `scale`, or `regex`), and `condition` (`pct <= threshold`) picks the
message; `{pct}` and `{threshold}` in a message print the number and the param.
Only add a probe you would run yourself: it is a command that reruns, cached, on
every later call until removed. The rules live in
`~/.config/vigil/advisories.toml` (re-read on every call; hand edits count).
Do not edit `boat-budget` unless the owner asked; a deleted default is not
brought back.

### Claude and Sol budget

Read each window separately. Claude has a 5-hour and a weekly limit; this
Codex plan currently has only a weekly limit. Use three advisories, each low
at 15% left or less:

- `claude-budget-5h`: wait for its reset or shift work to Sol for now.
- `claude-budget-weekly`: switch Claude's build-loop roles for the rest of the
  week, until the weekly reset.
- `codex-budget-weekly`: switch Sol's build-loop roles for the rest of the
  week, until the weekly reset.

`usage-budget-probe ClaudeCode --window 5h`, `usage-budget-probe ClaudeCode
--window weekly`, and `usage-budget-probe Codex --window weekly` report the
selected window's `pct_left`, `on_credits`, and `resets_at`. `windows` preserves
uw's window descriptor and duration. Without `--window`, the original keys
still describe the tightest window across the provider, so a combined reading
cannot tell you how long a role switch should last.

The owner or orchestrator adds these only when asked. Retire `claude-budget`
and `codex-budget` after adding the replacements to avoid contradictory role
advice. Probe argv accepts `--window` directly. Vigil message placeholders are
numeric, so name the window in the message and read reset timestamps from the
probe. Exit 3 means unavailable, including `no such window` when uw does not
report the requested duration. Treat unavailable as unknown and keep current
roles. A healthy 5-hour window never overrides a low weekly window; return to
default roles at a phase boundary only when every relevant window has recovered.
See build-loop's `references/budget.md`, B5.

## Going cold: the work is done

There is always a session to keep warm while work is in flight. The only cold
path is going from working or waiting to done. vigil never wakes or revives a
session, so when the work is done (or you are told to end the session), post
ONE collapsed BabelTele summary of the session inline in your final message and
end the turn. Call the MCP tool `cold` (or run `vigil cold ID...`) to cancel
your watches and holds; it replies with this instruction and the ids still
pending. Then stop calling vigil.
Never start a long cold wait instead: no background command that only waits for
something that may come much later, no sleeping until a result might arrive.

```
<details><summary>Session state (BabelTele)</summary>
task and its progress; work in flight (ids, paths, watch ids); tools in use
(MCP servers, CLIs such as vigil and qex); the user's standing rules for this
session; skills loaded
</details>
```

Use the `babeltele` skill to write it compactly.

## Fire rules

- `"change"`: any input changes from the baseline taken at create.
- `"condition"`: every input with a `want` meets it. Only `port`
  (`"open"`/`"closed"`) and `process` (`"exited"`/`"running"`) take `want`.
- `"judge"`: a Laya judge answers `judge_questions` and `judge_rule` decides.
  Needs `VIGIL_JUDGE_URL` and a reachable Laya (only on void).

```json
{"id": "build", "prompt": "Tell me when the build finishes or fails.",
 "inputs": [{"kind": "file", "path": "/tmp/build.log"},
            {"kind": "process", "pid": 4242, "want": "exited"}],
 "interval_s": 20, "deadline_s": 3600, "fire": "condition"}
```

Input kinds: `file`, `glob`, `cmd` (`argv`, `timeout_s` 0.1-19), `url`
(http only), `port`, `process`. Up to 16 inputs.

A glob input takes `pattern`, not `path`, and reports matches that appeared
since the last tick: `{"kind": "glob", "pattern": "/tmp/out/result*", "report": "created"}`.

A watch fires once. After a `change` (or `condition`, or `judge`) watch fires
it is finished: to keep watching, create a new watch with a fresh id. Ids of
finished watches cannot be reused until they are pruned (7 days).

## When the disk is full

vigil keeps its state on disk. If a write fails (usually a full disk), the
call still gives you the whole answer: `events`, `digest`, `status` and `next`
are the same as on a healthy disk. What changes is the `persist` field, which
a healthy call never has:

- `"persist": {"ok": false, "kind": "disk_full" | "io", "error": "...", "path": "..."}`:
  the result was NOT saved. `"redelivery": true` means events or a final status
  are at risk. `"first_error"` appears when a retry failed too.
- `"persist": {"ok": true, "used_reserve": true, "kind": "disk_full"}`: it was
  saved, but only by spending vigil's 256 KiB emergency reserve. The disk is
  full; free space soon.
- `"persist_failures": [{"watch_id", "kind", "error", "path"}]`: with several
  watches, other watches whose save failed in this call.

What to do:

- Act on the envelope as usual, then keep waiting. A tick that
  could not be saved is not saved, so the next call senses the change again.
  A quiet one (nothing to act on) makes the call wait one watch interval
  before it returns, so keep waiting: that wait is the pacing.
- Free space (the state root is `~/.local/state/vigil`; the CLI names it on
  stderr). The next healthy call saves and rebuilds the reserve.
- Treat any event that follows an envelope with `persist.ok = false` as
  possibly repeated. The MCP server (the process that failed to save) flags
  repeated events with `"redelivered": true`, and the same
  `event_id` can come back with different content, so do not deduplicate by
  `event_id`. A fresh CLI process (a new `vigil keepalive`) cannot know about the
  earlier failure, so its events are not flagged.
- `status` may lag: after a failed save `watch_status` can still say `pending`
  while `keepalive` answered `fired`. Trust the envelope.
- `watch_create` on a full disk fails with an error that names the state root
  and says `disk full`. Nothing is left behind, so retry with the same id once
  space is free.

What survives is best effort. `file` inputs redeliver what was appended since
the last saved tick, the newest `tail_bytes` of it (default 4096, never more
than 64 KiB; past 64 KiB the oldest bytes are skipped and the text says
`[truncated]`). `glob`, `cmd`, `url`, `port` and `process` report what they
see at the next tick (a glob its current matches), so a change that has
already reverted is not repeated. A watch that another process saved as expired or cancelled wins over
a redelivery. The reserve cannot help when the disk is out of inodes, a quota
is hit by a write bigger than 256 KiB, or the filesystem compresses zeros.

`VIGIL_TEST_FAULT` makes vigil's writes fail on purpose. It exists for vigil's
own tests and assumes a trusted environment: never set it, and be aware that
if it is inherited it disables writes (or, if malformed, stops vigil from
starting).

## Without MCP

```sh
echo '{...}' | vigil create      # prints the watch id
vigil keepalive build            # one call; add --orchestrator in the main session
vigil status build; vigil list; vigil cancel build
vigil advice [--json]            # the operator's current rules (see Advisories)
vigil hold [--id ID] [--for SPEC]... [--label L] [--expect-s N] [--until-idle]   # see Holds
vigil hold add ID --for SPEC [--label L] [--expect-s N]; vigil hold done ID LABEL
```

The CLI prints the envelope and then commits its delivery. If it cannot write
the envelope (stdout closed or full) it exits 1 and the next call returns the
undelivered events again, flagged `redelivered`.

## Client limits

- Claude Code moves a call longer than 2 min to a background task; the
  result still arrives, as a task notification. A 3000 s call (a background
  `vigil keepalive --orchestrator` run through Bash) needs a background timeout
  of at least 3,600,000 ms; with the default 10 minute limit it is killed.
- Codex caps a tool call at 300 s by default, and keepalive returns by 270 s
  (vigil never exceeds 270 s when it sees Codex, or both Codex and Claude).
  Kasetto cannot set `tool_timeout_sec`; to raise it, add
  `tool_timeout_sec = 330` under `[mcp_servers.vigil]` in
  `~/.codex/config.toml` yourself.

## Project reminders

For the owner's periodic technical reviews and comment audits, initialize the
current project once per session with adaptive-hardening's
`scripts/review-maintenance ensure --project ABS` (resolve the script relative
to that skill). It discovers new repositories as single-repository projects and
resolves configured multi-repository products to shared technical review history.
Each project gets `review-<key>` and `comment-audit-<key>` reminders with identical
scopes, split after 16 entries with matching `-2` and later ids. Rerun `ensure`
after scope or membership changes to refresh both kinds and retire obsolete
reminders. Grouping retires the former independent reminders too.
Use that skill's `group` command to associate additional repositories with a
product; do not infer membership from directory names.
Technical review reminders do not authorize paid work.

Comment audits deliver weekly on Saturday or Sunday, 09:00-21:00 in
America/Denver, the technical review reminder's timezone. Load `comment-audit`
and check headroom with `adaptive-hardening`. Audit files changed since the last
audit, or the whole repo once a month. Report only; edits need the owner. The
reminder authorizes at most lean work. It has no probe; each id's done state
suppresses its own weekly reminder.

Reminders deliver a project instruction only inside vigil calls you already
make. They never wake a session. Read `reminders` in keepalive/wait results and
`vigil advice --json` or MCP `advice`. Each due entry has an id and message;
`unavailable` means the check failed, so do not assume the reminder is due.
The list is absent outside the configured directory scopes, and empty within
scope when nothing is due. `reminders_error` reports an unreadable config file
whose scope cannot be established. Long main-session keepalives may return early with
`kind: "reminder_due"`, once per reminder per local day/week across sessions.
A reminder event leaves the watch live. Act on the message and follow `next`.

```sh
vigil remind list
vigil remind show ID          # spec plus current evaluation
vigil remind done ID          # suppress until the local day/week ends
vigil remind snooze ID 2h     # pause for an absolute duration, up to 7d
vigil remind rm ID
```

MCP: `remind_list`, `remind_show {id}`, `remind_add {id,spec}`,
`remind_done {id}`, `remind_snooze {id,duration}`, `remind_rm {id}`.
Configuration is `~/.config/vigil/reminders.toml` or the XDG config path,
re-read on calls. Suppression and cached probe output live under vigil's state
root. CLI scope follows the process cwd. MCP scope follows the server startup
cwd; roots and later client directory changes are not tracked. Use the CLI from
the project or restart the MCP server there.

An operator can install a scoped reminder. Use one timezone for its schedule
and probe:

```sh
reminder_tz=America/Denver
vigil remind add weekly-review \
  --scope /work/project --days wed,thu,fri --window 09:00-21:00 \
  --tz "$reminder_tz" --period week \
  --probe '["/work/project/bin/review-due"]' \
  --message 'A project review is due. {output}' --cache-s 21600 --timeout-s 19
```

Reminder delivery and the PreToolUse hook use the cache only. Cold/expired
results say unavailable while one spawned task refreshes eligible probes
concurrently within a single five-second deadline. Terminal watches and
outboxes are checked first. A short CLI may exit before refresh completes;
`vigil remind show ID` explicitly warms the cache. Failures last 60 seconds;
cache-only successful snapshots also have a 60-second minimum delivery lifetime.
The hook labels project reminders separately from operator advice.

`--window 09:00-18:00` optionally limits local delivery to that interval;
start is inclusive, end exclusive. Overnight windows are not supported in the
pilot. Omit `--tz` for host local time. Probe argv is JSON, with exit 0 due,
1 not due, other exits unavailable. Reserve exit 1 for a successful false
predicate, not a command error; it runs from the first scope. For a numeric
probe add `--condition 'value >= 100'`, optionally `--extract '<JSON>'` using
advisory extraction. `{output}` and `{value}` interpolate its result. Probes
have a timeout and cached results; add only commands you would run yourself.

# technical-excellence

Standards for what the code says and how it is shaped.

| Skill | Load it when |
|---|---|
| `test-quality` | Writing or reviewing the tests that prove an interface, claim or invariant here. |
| `build-loop` | The work is multi-phase, or a cross-model review will judge it. Its review step uses sections 6 and 7 below. |

First rule: **when in Rome.** Follow the repo's conventions (AGENTS.md,
existing style, lexicon) before anything below. Apply this skill where the repo
is silent.

## 1. Rich interfaces

An interface is more than signatures. Each abstraction documents:

| Part | Says |
|---|---|
| Error detail | What can fail, and how it is reported (type, code, null, exception). Callers must be able to handle each case without reading the body. |
| Reason | Why it exists. What breaks or duplicates if it is removed. |
| Invariants | What is always true before, during and after calls. |
| Mating parts | If it has a second or third counterpart (writer/reader, encoder/decoder, client/server), name them. |

**Mated parts need parity tests** proving both sides agree: round trip, plus
independent fixtures (see `test-quality`, parity and oracles). A pair that is
only tested against each other's constants proves nothing.

## 2. Claims are cited

Module-level comments and comments above code blocks contain verifiable
claims ("this is O(n)", "the device sends big-endian", "idempotent",
"commit happens before ACK"). Every such claim is anchored and sourced.

Convention (adapt the comment syntax to the language):

```
// CLAIM(ack-order): the commit completes before the ACK is sent [spec §4.2; ack_order_test]
...
// ↳ CLAIM(ack-order)
ack(token);
```

- The comment states a **verifiable** claim and its **source or proof** in
  brackets: a spec section, capture file, proof sketch, or test name.
- The code the claim governs carries `↳ CLAIM(<id>)`.
- A maintainer changing that code greps the id, finds the claim and its
  proof, and re-checks it.
- Tests that prove the claim name the id in their why (`test-quality`).
- Ids are short, unique, stable. Unprovable "claims" are opinions: label them
  as such or delete them. A comment with no source is a rumor.

Comments that are not claims or interface contracts are smells
(`comment-audit`). Never write a note from your session into a comment
("added for ticket 4", "now uses X", "as requested"); that belongs in the
commit message. A comment that excuses a workaround in our own code marks
code to reshape, not explain. A decision's why that spans modules goes in an
ADR, and the site carries `ADR-NNNN`.

## 3. Deep modules

Prefer a simple interface over a substantial implementation. Few entry
points, few parameters, no leaked internals. Smells: shallow wrappers that
forward one call; interfaces as long as the body; callers that must know
call order. Hide the complexity; do not spread it across callers.

## 4. Lexicon and naming

Keep a project lexicon (a glossary doc: term, meaning, where it lives). Name
code in correspondence with it. Add a term to the glossary when you coin one;
do not use two words for one concept. Where the project uses residual, its
lexicon is the source; how terms are tested and which near-synonyms to avoid
belong to the lexicon, not here (`question-everything` §1a).

Outside any convention:

- Clear names, **no abbreviations**.
- 1-2 primary words, plus optional small words (determiners, prepositions):
  `rowsToPrune`, `nightOfRecord`.
- Be deliberate about grammar:
  - functions and methods: verbs (`parseFrame`); predicates read as
    questions (`isFinalized`, `hasPendingWrite`);
  - values and types: nouns (`dayLabel`, `HistoryToken`);
  - qualifiers: adjectives (`pendingRows`);
  - tense shows state: `committedRows` (done), `rowsToCommit` (not yet).
- Name by how the value is used, not its type. Avoid vague names such as
  `value`, `data`, `result`, `tmp`. A function that sums two numbers returns
  `sum`; a truly generic result is `returnValue`.

## 5. Type-level safety first

Algorithmic and algebraic design shrinks runtime checks, tests and review.
Reach for these before adding a check:

| Tool | Effect |
|---|---|
| Make invalid states unrepresentable (sum types, non-empty lists, state enums carrying only valid fields) | The bug cannot compile. No test or review needed. |
| Newtypes / branded types (`LocalDayLabel` vs `UtcTimestamp`, `Milliseconds` vs `Seconds`) | Mixed-up units and ids fail to compile. |
| Exhaustive matching, no default branch | Adding a case forces every consumer to be updated. |
| Monoids (identity, associative combine) for accumulators | Split-merge equals single pass; parallelism and incrementality are safe. Prove laws with property tests (`test-quality`). |
| Parse, don't validate: convert raw input to a checked type once, at the boundary | Inner code never re-checks. |
| Smart constructors, private fields | Invariants hold by construction. |

If a runtime check or a test exists only to catch an invalid state a type
could forbid, change the type.

## 6. Security stance review

Security judgments are made against a **threat model**, never by reflex.

1. Use the project's existing framework (a residual-risk framework, AGENTS.md
   invariants, an existing model).
2. If none exists, write a short `THREAT_MODEL.md`: assets, actors, trust
   boundaries, in scope, out of scope. Leave it UNCOMMITTED unless the user
   says otherwise.
3. Question the stance itself: which assets matter most, who can reach which
   boundary, what is knowingly accepted. Record accepted risks with a reason.
4. For each security-relevant change or review comment, decide: real exposure
   under the model, hardening nicety, or out of scope. State which and why.
5. Where a project limits reviewers to correctness findings, honor that for
   what you ask of them, but still assess security yourself.

## 7. Judging review findings

A finding is not a nit because it is small. Check it against: the claim it
contradicts (section 2), the invariant it breaks (section 1), the type that
could prevent it (section 5), and the threat model (section 6). Then apply
the smallest fix, with a test that fails without it (`test-quality`).
