# A visual language for Farhan notifications

Start with two views of the same notification. Inbox should show what happened and retain the original message. Overview should show when Farhan may deliver it and what could hold it back. When six separate posts come from one chat, Inbox can show one conversation and Overview can account for six entries. Those views can share the underlying records without implying that their counts mean the same thing.

## Recommendations

1. Try cards by kind in Inbox, starting with conversations where Farhan has a stable thread ID and a plain row for everything else. Keep the original notification a tap away.
2. Try a delivery timeline in Overview. Mark the next eligible batch and show the current points available. Label a forecast as an estimate and give budget holds a separate state.

## What the owner's research contributes

- **Give each object ways to explain itself.** In Glamorous Toolkit, Phlow discovers inspector views declared on an object's class and its superclasses. Each view can decide whether it applies to the object. One object can expose a list, a tree, a graph, raw text, or a small hand-built view. In Farhan, the same notification can answer “What happened?”, “Why is it waiting?” and “What did the app actually send?” from the same record. The kind chooses the first view. Available evidence determines which details it can show. [Portable moldable components, §1 and §3](../../mstack/research/11-moldable-components.md) · [phoe-nix copy](../../phoe-nix/knowledge/research/agentic-practice-2026-11/11-moldable-components.md) · [GT inspector views](https://book.gtoolkit.com/inspector-views-59974yxnj0txylwrjryp4uc1b)
- **Make each view answer one question and keep the next question reachable.** Gîrba’s contextual micro-tool answers a question from the domain itself and provides a path to the facts it used. The owner's README makes this a test for keeping a component. GT can combine views, forward a view from a related object, and open the selected object in an adjacent inspector. On a phone, a batch can open its members, a conversation can open the individual posts, and an item can open its delivery details and original text. Back returns to the same place. [mstack README, How I approach agent work](../../mstack/README.md) · [Gîrba, Wayne and O’Reilly, §1](../../mstack/research/18-girba-wayne-oreilly.md) · [Moldable development, Questions attached to working tools](../../mstack/research/03-moldable-development.md) · [The Moldable Inspector](https://scg.unibe.ch/archive/papers/Chis15a-MoldableInspector.pdf)
- **Compose views over the same facts.** The owner’s paneweft design separates the renderer, the named view definition for a domain kind, and the snapshot the view displays. Its proposed Vigil example gives the same watch a lifecycle view, an events list, and a tested example. Paneweft documents a working path for typed views declared beside Rust or TypeScript code and collected from real test values. Browser and text projections use the same captured facts. Farhan can use the same pattern with a few shared Compose elements and a closed set of trusted presentation types. A compact status strip and an expanded list should agree about how many items are waiting. [paneweft README, v1](../../paneweft/README.md#v1-views-and-examples-that-live-in-the-code) · [paneweft design, Inspector model](../../paneweft/docs/design.md#3-inspector-model) · [In-code views, §3 and §6](../../mstack/research/12-paneweft-v1-in-code-views.md) · [phoe-nix copy](../../phoe-nix/knowledge/research/agentic-practice-2026-11/12-paneweft-v1-in-code-views.md)
- **Use inspectable examples and give a reason.** A GT example checks a behavior and returns the object so its views stay available for inspection and reuse. In the gt4llm follow-up, the owner revises the earlier suggestion to split human and agent views. Paneweft already renders one record to browser and text, and the owner proposes sibling decision views that expose the candidates and the reason for the choice. Farhan's equivalent is a fixed-clock example that checks the six-message queue, exposes the cards and next eligible batch, and lets the owner inspect why one item missed that batch. “Why?” should read the same policy inputs that produced the estimate. [gt4llm and liveness tests, §1.4 and §1.7](../../mstack/research/20-gt4llm-and-liveness-tests.md) · [Views that teach, Showing the thinking](../../mstack/research/13-research-direction-views-that-teach.md) · [Example-driven development](https://arxiv.org/html/2409.00514v1)

## What Farhan already knows

The Inbox has priority filters, a Cleared view, paging, and an individually keyed list. Each rendered item has source, title, body, time, a priority rail, and a textual priority and category. A channel label and original actions appear when available. The existing tap, context menu and per-item dismiss behavior are the starting point for the card pilot. The current capture shows the original Inbox chrome with an empty list under an onboarding overlay. The schedule captures show the existing time axis and point windows, and the App Priorities captures show priority chips at list scale. The HTML baseline draws populated rows from the source and uses the owner's chosen bottom bar for all three samples. [Inbox screen][inbox] · [Inbox row][row] · [Current Inbox](../captures/notifications/farhan-current.png) · [Schedule editor](../captures/notifications/farhan-pilot-editor.png) · [App Priorities](../captures/notifications/farhan-runtime-profile-after/categories.png) · [Navigation mock-up](settings-nav-mockups.html)

The stored timestamp comes from Android's post time. The item has delivery, read, cleared, and invalidation flags and a priority reason. It has no general structured payload for calendar events, payments, progress, stable conversations, or repeats. A channel groups an app's notification settings and can span many conversations. A delivery time should come from an observed send record, where available. A successful post records Farhan handing the notification to Android. Read status remains separate. The dashboard's Recent Batches clusters posts by source and time range. Those clusters can supply expansion and paging patterns. [Item model][item] · [Notification intake][service] · [Recent Batches aggregation][batches] · [Delivery coordinator][coordinator] · [Android channels](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/views/notifications/channels)

The default cadences are immediate for Critical, hourly for High, every other hour for Medium, and daily at midnight for Low. Critical bypasses the budget by default. The nominal point costs are 0, 2, 4 and 8 respectively. Actual cost follows the applicable budget behavior. For batched priorities, the next cadence tick gives the earliest opportunity under the cadence. The queue order, active schedule and points, hourly limit, and delivery gates affect actual delivery. Keep the priority on the stored item used by the delivery policy distinct from the effective priority the Inbox shows for old unread items. [Priority defaults][settings] · [Point costs][priority] · [Delivery policy][policy] · [Delivery clock context][clock] · [Delivery coordinator][coordinator] · [Inbox priority filter][filter]

## Vocabulary

| Dimension | Encoding on a phone | Source or limit |
|---|---|---|
| Priority | A fixed-position marker plus the full priority word. A triangle marks Critical, a diamond High, a square Medium, and a circle Low. Use red, amber, blue and gray as secondary cues. | Show the applicable Farhan priority. Android channel importance and Farhan priority are two different settings. |
| Category and kind | Use a glyph next to the subject, such as a bubble for a conversation, a calendar for an event, or a box for a shipment. Keep the category word in details and accessible names. | Use Farhan's broad category for a fallback. Choose a specialized view when its own fields are present. |
| Source app | Put the app name in the same place on every card or row. Show an app icon where available. | Use package identity for grouping and a distinct profile scope where multiple profiles are admitted. |
| Chattiness | Show a count beside the app and a short strip of arrivals on a common time scale in Overview. | Count distinct recorded posts in a stated interval. Label the interval and any coverage gaps. |
| Arrival vs. delivery | Show “Posted 10:31” and “Delivered 10:39” or “Estimated 11:00.” A time axis can mark a post with a hollow dot, an observed send with a solid dot, and a forecast with a dashed mark. | Use the source post time and the separately recorded send time. Where a legacy item only has a delivered flag, show “Delivered” without a time. |
| Time waiting | Show “Waiting 11 min” beside the forecast. On a detail timeline, the span from post to now shows elapsed age while pending. | This is age since posting unless Farhan records a separate intake time. Stop the clock after delivery or invalidation. |
| Budget cost | Use a figure with units on batch headers and details, such as “12 pts.” On Overview, show spent and available as segments with numbers. | Distinguish observed spend, projected spend, and budget bypass. A larger cost never makes a notification visually more urgent. |
| Thread membership | Expand a stack headed “Weekend hike · 6 messages.” Show the latest sender and snippet first. | Use a stable conversation identifier where available. An app bucket is labelled with the app's name and notification count. |
| Expects action | A label such as “Review activity” sits next to the reported alert when the source provides a matching action or explicit request. Put it on a full-size target when the action is available. | Label the sender's request and use existing supported actions. Missing action metadata leaves the original content as the way to find out. |
| Repeats | A loop glyph and a count such as “4 repeats in 24 h” belong on a collapsed series. | Require a stable series key or a documented, inspectable grouping rule. Distinguish an update to one post from a new repeat. |
| Next eligible delivery | A local time heads each group on a vertical list. In Overview a shared time scale lets priority lanes show the next tick. Put “Waiting for budget” or “Delivery unavailable” in a labelled group when appropriate. | Recompute when settings or queue state change. Include the date beyond today. The forecast and its reason come from the same snapshot. |

Keep the first line readable with one hand and use the whole row for the main tap. Use a 48 dp target for a disclosure or explicit action. Allow labels to wrap at large font sizes and provide an accessible summary for drawn marks; at narrow widths the timeline can read as a vertical list. Check both Material color schemes and grayscale. Use shape, label, and position as redundant cues. Reserve movement for an optional transition when state changes and keep all meaning visible with reduced motion. Keep message text, sender names, amounts as posted, and event details as text. [Compose accessibility defaults](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/accessibility/api-defaults)

## What other interfaces lend Farhan

| Example | Idea and application |
|---|---|
| Android Material 3 Expressive | Shape, type and motion can make hierarchy easier to see. Give an exceptional Critical item a distinct silhouette and leave the rest at a stable rhythm. [Material 3 in Compose](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/designsystems/material3) |
| Compose Canvas | Draw marks on a scale with `Canvas` and keep row labels and touch targets in Compose layout. Use this for cadence ticks and arrival strips. [Graphics in Compose](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/graphics/draw/overview) |
| Jetpack Glance | Glance uses a Compose-based API for Android app widgets. Its compact layout suggests “Next batch 11:00 · 5 items” as a self-contained Overview card. [Jetpack Glance](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/glance) |
| Wear OS Tiles and complications | A tile gives quick access to a focused view and a complication fits a small fact on the watch face. Model the Overview card as a next-time/count pair that opens coverage and budget details. [Wear OS surfaces](https://developer.android.com/training/wearables/user-interfaces) |
| Android 16 progress-centric notifications and Live Updates | ProgressStyle offers segments and points for stages in an ongoing activity. In Farhan, show “Out for delivery” and the next stage when the source supplies a meaningful sequence. Use separate text for Farhan’s own delivery time. [ProgressStyle on Android 16](https://developer.android.com/about/versions/16/features/progress-centric-notifications) · [Live Updates](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/notifications/live-update) |
| Android grouping and conversations | A notification group can expand into children, and MessagingStyle carries conversation-specific structure. Use one thread card for six verified messages with each source post still inspectable. [Groups](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/views/notifications/group) · [Conversations](https://developer.android.com/social-and-messaging/guides/communication/notifications-conversations) |
| Android channels and importance | Android importance controls how interruptive a channel's notifications are. Borrow a labelled importance glyph for a Farhan priority, with channel policy visible in details as its own setting. [Notification channels](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/views/notifications/channels) |
| iOS Live Activities and Dynamic Island | A single evolving activity has compact and expanded presentations. Show a short shipment stage in the Inbox and open a richer view of that shipment where there is evidence for more. [Live Activities](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/live-activities) |
| iOS Scheduled Summary and Focus | Scheduled Summary batches selected apps at chosen times. Focus can also select people or apps that can notify and filter supported apps’ content. Let Farhan show the active schedule and the next batch’s membership and explain any applicable exception. [Scheduled Summary](https://support.apple.com/guide/iphone/view-and-respond-to-notifications-iph6534c01bc/ios) · [Focus filters](https://support.apple.com/en-euro/guide/iphone/iphd6288a67f/26/ios/26) |
| Slack Block Kit | An application assembles messages from blocks suited to the surface. Use named card parts such as subject, status, source, and action in a few local templates. [Block Kit](https://docs.slack.dev/reference/block-kit/) |
| Microsoft Adaptive Cards | A JSON card describes content and the host renders it in its own style. A verified payment payload could fill an amount and merchant template that inherits Farhan’s theme. [Adaptive Cards](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/adaptive-cards/) |
| Observable Plot and Vega-Lite | Marks encode fields through positions, lengths and other channels, and facets repeat the same plotting frame. Draw source activity as equal-scale rows, with the same hourly bins for every app. [Observable Plot marks](https://observablehq.github.io/plot/features/marks) · [Vega-Lite facets](https://vega.github.io/vega-lite/docs/facet.html) |
| Tufte sparklines and small multiples | A small series can sit beside its label and final value. Repeat the same scale for each app, and label a count such as “13 posts in 2 h” beside the strip so a burst remains legible without reading the whole series. [Sparkline theory and practice](https://www.edwardtufte.com/notebook/sparkline-theory-and-practice-edward-tufte/) · [Clinical data display example](https://www.edwardtufte.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/Summarizing-Clinical-Psychiatric-Data-Seth-M-Powsner-Edward-R-Tufte.pdf) |
| Gantt charts and git graphs | A Gantt chart aligns spans against a time axis, and a git graph keeps distinct histories in lanes. Use budget windows as spans and priorities as lanes. Use an explicit link to its source post when a send mark can be paired with it. [Mermaid Gantt](https://mermaid.js.org/syntax/gantt) · [Mermaid gitGraph](https://mermaid.js.org/syntax/gitgraph) |
| Superhuman | Split Inbox puts messages that match a rule into their own view. Let a review pass bring “Waiting for budget” together with an explicit rule and an item count. [Custom Split Inbox](https://help.superhuman.com/hc/en-us/articles/46005636204941-Custom-Split-Inbox) |
| HEY Imbox | Imbox, Feed and Paper Trail give people separate places for correspondence, things to browse, and receipts. Give recurring news and transaction receipts compact group headers inside Farhan’s chosen Inbox, using explicit rules. [The Imbox](https://help.hey.com/article/759-imbox) · [HEY mail views](https://help.hey.com/article/903-how-can-i-see-all-my-emails) |
| Gmail categories | Default Inbox categories can group mail automatically, and users can move a misfiled message. A Farhan kind view could expose its fallback and allow a deliberate override if kinds prove useful. [Gmail categories](https://support.google.com/mail/answer/3094499) |
| Linear Triage | Incoming issues await a decision such as accept or decline. Borrow the visible pending state for cases where the user can genuinely decide what happens next. [Linear Triage](https://linear.app/docs/triage) |
| Things and Todoist | Things can drop a captured task into Inbox for later organization. Todoist’s Inbox is the default home for a task with no project. A quiet Farhan row can stay readable before the user decides whether to open or clear it. [Things Quick Entry](https://culturedcode.com/things/support/articles/2249437/) · [Todoist Inbox](https://www.todoist.com/help/todoist/get-started/use-the-inbox-in-todoist-HwHvYErS) |
| Bloomberg Terminal | Bloomberg’s Launchpad shows market monitors, charts and alerts in a workspace that updates in place. A compact Farhan panel can line up each source’s arrival count, pending count and points in the same columns. Keep the long text one tap away. [Bloomberg’s Launchpad design](https://www.bloomberg.com/company/stories/innovating-a-modern-icon-how-bloomberg-keeps-the-terminal-cutting-edge/) |
| Apple Watch glanceables | A complication fits a small fact into a watch-face slot. An Overview header can give one number and its unit, such as “10 pts left,” with the window printed beside it. [Apple complications](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/complications) |
| Teenage Engineering OP-1 | The hardware uses repeated symbols and shared color across related functions. Give a handful of Farhan kinds fixed silhouettes and repeat them where their meaning stays the same. [OP-1 mode controls](https://teenage.engineering/guides/op-1/original/main-modes) |
| Material Symbols | Fill, weight and optical size are separate axes. Let fill denote a selected control and tune weight for legibility at small sizes. Keep priority encoded by its own shape and label. [Material Symbols guide](https://developers.google.com/fonts/docs/material_symbols) |
| Traffic lights | The vertical red, yellow, green order adds a positional cue. Keep the location and shape of Farhan priority markers consistent and put the priority name beside them. [FHWA MUTCD, Part 4](https://mutcd.fhwa.dot.gov/pdfs/11th_Editionr1/part4r1.pdf) |
| TCAS | Traffic Collision Avoidance System displays distinguish a filled yellow circle for a traffic advisory from a filled red square for a resolution advisory. The transferable idea is redundant shape and color for states requiring different responses. Farhan can use its own labelled priority shapes. [FAA TCAS II introduction](https://www.faa.gov/documentLibrary/media/Advisory_Circular/TCAS%20II%20V7.1%20Intro%20booklet.pdf) |
| Aviation annunciators and master caution | A common attention cue prompts the crew to look for a specific labelled condition. Show one persistent “Budget blocked” or “Flood active” cue in Overview. Open the rows affected and state why. [FAA Flightcrew Alerting](https://www.faa.gov/documentLibrary/media/Advisory_Circular/AC_25.1322-1.pdf) |

## Five display languages

| Language | Inbox and Overview rule | Makes easy | Hides or costs attention | Fit for Farhan |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cards by kind | Give the item a view that answers its kind's main question. Overview counts posts by kind using the same glyphs and opens a scoped Inbox. | Read a thread once, see the time of an event or identify what a bank alert is asking. | Card heights vary. Group headers hide earlier snippets until opened. | One thumb can open a whole card. A few templates share priority marks and a plain fallback. |
| Delivery timeline | Inbox groups pending items by estimated delivery and shows delivered items separately. Overview aligns priority lanes and budget windows. | Answer “When will this show up?” and see the one message that misses 11:00. | Separates related posts when only some fit a batch. Clock and date labels need room. | Makes cadence and budget visible inside the chosen navigation. A vertical list works on a narrow phone. |
| Source activity strips | Inbox shows equal-height app groups with count and latest subject. Overview adds small multiples of arrivals, with shared time bins and numeric counts. | Trace who produced a burst and spot which app stayed quiet. | Compresses the content and can blur separate conversations. One app may dominate a shared scale. | Useful at flood scale and legible without color. Whole rows open the posts. |
| Quiet list | Inbox shows source, subject and time on one or two lines with a small labelled priority cue. Overview shows the next eligible batch and the number waiting, with details on tap. | Scroll quickly and find a specific subject with little visual noise. | The body, exact budget, reason for waiting, and related items need another tap. | Lowest Compose cost and a comfortable dense mode. Keep visible text at large font sizes by letting rows grow. |
| Triage by exception | Inbox groups verified requests for action and explicit delivery exceptions first, with the remaining items in a dated list. Overview shows a labelled condition and its count only while it applies. | Find something the user can act on, such as a verified bank review request or a queue blocked by a full window. | A false action signal harms trust. A routine event may move further down the screen. | Suits standing alarms and flood status with an evidence-based trigger. Priority and “requires action” remain separate facts. |

### What the cards render

| Kind | First view and fallback |
|---|---|
| Message thread | Stack by source and stable thread identity. Lead with the latest sender and snippet. Expand to original posts. Without an identity, show independent rows or a labelled app bucket. |
| Payment | Put amount, currency and merchant as reported on one line, with the source and event time below. Prefer the generic row when fields are ambiguous or absent. |
| Calendar | Put the source-reported local event time next to the title. Keep its location and the source post time labelled separately. |
| Delivery update | Put the current shipment stage first. Show a stage strip and the source ETA if those fields are available. |
| Alert | Start with the reported condition and what the sender asks. Surface an action only where Farhan has a supported action reference. |
| One-time code | Show a labelled masked code. Keep any reveal in the individual item and keep codes out of aggregates and previews. Use a known kind or trustworthy source metadata. |
| Generic | Show original app, title, text, post time and priority. An unknown kind retains the same access to delivery details. |

For a pilot, the existing category and captured data can support a generic card and category marks. Android’s notification API can expose a shortcut ID, style extras and progress where apps publish them. It offers no common typed schema for arbitrary bank, parcel and calendar messages. Add narrow capture rules at intake and select a specialized card only when evidence is sufficient. Keep classification read-only with respect to delivery. The mock-up assumes usable thread, calendar, parcel and code fields for the demo. It groups six distinct records. A single MessagingStyle notification containing six message lines would still be one queued record and incur at most one charge on delivery. [Android Notification API](https://developer.android.com/reference/android/app/Notification) · [Android conversations](https://developer.android.com/social-and-messaging/guides/communication/notifications-conversations) · [Current intake][service] · [Delivery policy][policy]

## Compose cost and reuse

### Cards by kind in Inbox

Low to medium cost for a generic card and one verified thread variant, roughly 2–4 developer days for a pilot once the source metadata is settled. Keep `LazyColumn`, existing row actions, filters and `NotificationListItem` as the fallback. Borrow expand, page and open behavior from `RecentBatchesWidget`. Reuse `CategoryBreakdownWidget` for category totals and the weighted segments in `PriorityDistributionWidget` for a compact count display. The mock-up’s counts by presentation kind would need their own aggregation. Cost increases if thread grouping has to span pages, or if kind-specific data needs a storage migration. Keep one canonical item ID and individual dismiss/read behavior within a group. Start with the verified conversation and defer transaction, parcel, calendar and code renderers until useful metadata is demonstrated. [Inbox screen][inbox] · [Existing row][row] · [Recent Batches][recentWidget] · [Category Breakdown][categoryWidget] · [Priority Distribution][distWidget]

### Delivery timeline in Overview

Medium cost for a next-opportunity card by priority, roughly 2–3 developer days if it shows only cadence ticks and the active balance. Reuse the cadence settings from `PriorityDeliveryWidget`, windows from `NotificationScheduleWidget`, and the balance and progress indicator from `BudgetSpendWidget`. Use Compose text for times, amounts and tap routes, with a small Canvas or ordinary Compose layout for lines and marks. Keep the dashboard's existing top-chatter and standing sections available. A forecast that assigns individual rows to batches is higher cost, roughly a week for a bounded pilot. It needs a coherent read-only snapshot, explicit eligibility and hold reasons, and parity with coordinator ordering, live-source gating and limits. Project a bounded horizon and show “Waiting for budget” or “No estimate” beyond it. Refresh on queue, budget, schedule, time zone or clock changes. Ignore stale forecasts and use the dated schedule that applies to each future day. Recent Batches can supply its disclosure pattern. Its source-grouped post timestamps cannot identify the delivery history. The current spend log timestamps charged sends and lacks an item ID. A precise per-item history wou

The Inbox mock includes the delivery view to test whether it is worth opening from Overview. I would start with the two surfaces above and keep the choice of a second full Inbox mode open. The sample is a 10:42 snapshot with default cadences, newest-first chat ordering, and a custom budget. Five High items can use the remaining 10 points at 11:00. The sixth waits for 12:00, when it and two Medium items use 10 of the new 12 points. The Low item can use 8 of 10 points at midnight. The spend at 10:42 comes from earlier items already cleared from the Inbox. The illustrative forecast assumes no further arrivals, cancellations, delivery failures or other gate changes.

## Questions for the owner

1. When you reach for Inbox after a busy hour, do you want to catch up by conversation or see what Farhan is still holding?
2. Should the timeline say “Next eligible at 11:00” first, or is it worth estimating which five messages can fit then?
3. Can verified chat threads collapse by default? For apps with weak metadata, do you prefer independent rows or an explicit app bucket?
4. Which would earn a second renderer after chat? A bank alert, an appointment, a shipment, or a one-time code?
5. How much should an Inbox card reveal for bank and code notifications before you open it?

The [HTML comparison](notification-display-mockups.html) uses a fictional queue and the dark palette from [the navigation mock-up](settings-nav-mockups.html). The code and captures support the baseline and the policy inputs. Specialized intake coverage, the forecast’s runtime accuracy and the layouts on a device remain unmeasured. The HTML received a markup read-through and structure check. Browser rendering, TalkBack and light theme remain unverified.

content.text:
The display-language research is back, and the mock-ups above are its first draft. I haven't redrawn them myself, so treat them as a proposal. Nothing has been built.

**Recommendation:**
- **Inbox:** group a chat's messages into one card by kind where Farhan can tell they belong to the same conversation. Everything else stays a plain row, and the original notification is one tap away.
- **Overview:** add a delivery timeline. It marks the next batch, the points left, and which notifications are waiting only because of the budget, separate from a forecast.

The idea comes from your Glamorous Toolkit work: each notification can answer "what happened", "why is it waiting" and "what did the app send" from the same record. The mock-ups use the same 11 sample notifications in all three views, so they compare fairly.

The researcher did not check the layout in a browser or on a device.

**For you to pick:**
1. Should I try both ideas, or only one first?
2. Should the cards and timeline come in with the settings menu and bottom bar, or after? I'd do them after, since both touch the screens that build is changing.

If you pick one, I'll redraw it in the Farhan style at phone width and run it through the same mock-up-to-build comparison.

Delegated task node:delegated-task:command%3Amcp%3Aa9583e5f-0f51-4b45-be2b-5bf111e74c2e%3Athread-send%3A6412e51c-a3ec-47bc-9a2e-7561ab9b9353 (Review: per-category Clear and usage-permission fix (Opus)) [completed]:
Three answers from the code. I edited nothing.

**1. You're right about proxies; I withdraw finding 5 as written.**
- **A source cancel leaves the proxy posted.** In `NotificationService.kt:328-341`, a source-app removal does `captureEvent(originalId, removed = true)`, then `actionStore.remove`, then `Work.Removed`. At `:84` that becomes `coordinator.onRemoved`, which calls `rows.markCleared(id)` (`NotificationDeliveryCoordinator.kt:200`). Nothing on that path calls `cancelProxy`. So a row that Farhan already delivered and the source app then cancels sits in Cleared with its proxy still posted. Mark-as-cleared (`clearInbox`, `:207`) does cancel the proxy through `deleteNotificationIntent`. Arrival-side `markCleared` (`:174`, `:253`, `:272`, `:283`) happens before or instead of a post. But the source-cancel path alone disproves "cleared rows have no proxies". The Cleared clear has to keep cancelling proxies.
- **Invalidation for Cleared rows is mostly redundant, but harmless to keep.** Every path above records an event with `removed = true`, so `stale()` already rejects any callback captured before the removal. The only extra thing `invalidateDeleted` does for a cleared ID is drop a fresh re-post captured after the removal but before the press. Without the clear, that post would revive the row. That's a narrow edge, so I'm downgrading it to a nit. Keeping one code path for every scope is simpler. Don't special-case Cleared.
- **The cost is the binder calls, not the loop.** `NotificationManager.cancel(tag, id)` is an IPC every time, because the client can't know whether the ID is posted. The loop already runs in one gate hold with no per-ID suspension: `clearActions(ids)` is a plain function called once inside `NonCancellable`. So batching is already in place and changes nothing. The cheap fix that works for every scope:
  - read `manager.activeNotifications` once, the same pattern `cancelAllProxies` uses;
  - intersect it with `ids` and cancel only those (live proxies are capped at `MAX_LIVE_PROXIES = 1024`);
  - remove the retained actions for every ID in memory.

  That gives one IPC plus at most the live proxies. Severity: should, keyed to how large history can grow, which I didn't measure.

**2. Agreed: decline finding 6.** All behaves the same way, and a row that arrives while the gate is busy can't be told apart from one that arrives a moment after the press. A one-line note in the report is enough.

**3. The flash is new in this branch.** At base 717faf6, `NotificationFilterViewModel.kt:149-158`:
```kotlin
is NotificationFilterEvent.OnSetPriorityFilter -> {
    state = state.copy(priorityFilter = event.priority)
    state = state.copy(page = 0)
    getNotifications()
}
...
NotificationFilterEvent.OnToggleClearedView -> {
    state = state.copy(showCleared = !state.showCleared, page = 0)
    getNotifications()
}
```
Base kept the old list until the new query emitted. This branch adds `filteredNotifications = emptyList(), clearedNotifications = emptyList()` at `:142` and `:150`. The empty list is what triggers "No notifications" (`Screen:259`), so it's in scope.

The branch has a reason for hiding the list: it stops the user from pressing "Clear high" while the Low list is still on screen. The fix is a loading state, not reverting the blanking: render nothing and hide the button until the first emission.

**Revised verdicts:**
- **A: CHANGES** (findings 1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 8, plus finding 5 reworked as the one-IPC proxy cancel). Correctness 7, concurrency 8, tests 6, legibility 7.
- **B: OK** with the should-fixes you accepted. Correctness 9, concurrency 10, tests 5, legibility 8.

# Review round 1 (Opus) of fix/clear-per-category 10dd0d1, with orchestrator decisions

Verdict CHANGES, no musts. Correctness 7, concurrency 8, tests 6, legibility 7. The core is sound: one SQL predicate (`INBOX_PREDICATE`) for list, id selection and delete; select+delete in one Room transaction inside the gate with `NonCancellable`; deleted ids = invalidated ids; `:app:compileDebugKotlin` passes.

## Fix now (should)

1. `NotificationFilterState.kt:25` `showCleared -> Cleared(priorityFilter)` and `NotificationFilterScreen.kt:238`: tapping Cleared deselects the priority chips but the hidden `priorityFilter` stays, so "Delete cleared history" deletes only that priority's cleared rows (and the list shows only them). Fix: `OnToggleClearedView` sets `priorityFilter = null` when entering Cleared; `InboxClearScope.Cleared` then carries no priority. Test: select Low, open Cleared, assert list and clear scope both cover all priorities.
2. No ViewModel routing test (`NotificationFilterViewModel.kt:122`, `:85`). Add one with a fake repository/use case: select Low, let a page arrive, dispatch the clear, assert the use case received `Priority(LOW)` and the query's own `standingCutoff`. It must fail if the handler calls the old global clear, and fail if the cutoff is 0. Name the mutation in `catches:`.
3. `strings.xml`: the All label lost its translations (core `R.string.clear_all`, translated in ca, fr, ar, es, pl, ta). Keep core's `clear_all` for the All scope (or carry the translations over). New scope strings may be English only; say so in the report.
4. `NotificationFilterViewModel.kt:142`/`:150` (new in this branch; base kept the old list until the new query emitted): blanking the lists makes the screen show "No notifications" and hides the Clear button on every chip tap. Keep the blanking (it stops "Clear High" while Low is on screen) but add a loading state: render nothing and hide the button until the first emission for the new query. Test the state without Compose.
5. Cleared-history clear is thousands of per-id `NotificationManager.cancel` IPCs. Do not special-case Cleared (a source cancel leaves the proxy posted and marks the row Cleared, so cleared rows can have live proxies; keep one code path for all scopes). Instead read `manager.activeNotifications` once (the pattern `cancelAllProxies` uses), intersect with the deleted ids, cancel only those; remove retained actions for every deleted id in memory. Live proxies are capped at `MAX_LIVE_PROXIES = 1024`. Test with a fake manager that records cancels: only active ids are cancelled, all ids' actions are removed.

## Fix now (nits, small)

6. Reset `page = 0` after a clear (clearing Low from page 3 must not land on an empty page 3 with Newer enabled).
7. `NotificationDeliveryCoordinatorTest`: pin the `event.order <= clearOrder` guard (`:226`). Capture an event inside the `delete` lambda and assert its arrival is accepted (a post captured during `delete()` must not be dropped). Mutation: remove the guard, test must fail.
8. Rename `DeleteAllNotifications` to `ClearInbox`; make `ownProxy` in `NotificationRemovalMapper` required (no default); pass the same query shape (without paging, including `search`) in `NotificationRepositoryImpl.kt:61` instead of hardcoding `search = ""`.

## Declined (orchestrator, with reviewer's agreement)

- High-water mark for rows arriving between press and gate: the old All clear behaved the same, and such a row is indistinguishable from one arriving a moment later. Put one sentence in the report as a known limit.

## Evidence

Run the targeted tests on Boat again (domain, data, presentation, plus `:app:compileDebugKotlin`). Do the 30-minute flag. Commit as a new commit on the branch (do not amend 10dd0d1); `test-quality` rules apply (why/catches, no loosened assertions). Update `research/clear-category-report.md`.

NotificationListenerService.requestListenerHints (HINT_HOST_DISABLE_EFFECTS, HINT_HOST_DISABLE_NOTIFICATION_EFFECTS, HINT_HOST_DISABLE_CALL_EFFECTS): what exactly it suppresses today on API 35 (sound, vibration, lights, heads-up?), whether it is global or per notification, who may call it, whether it needs any grant beyond notification access, when it is cleared (listener disconnect, process death, reboot), and whether it interacts with the user's interruption filter. Include the Automatic Zen rule route (AutomaticZenRule) as an alternative that leaves the user's manual DND alone.

5. A recommended design with a failure analysis: what happens if the hint is on and Farhan's process dies (does the phone go silent?), at reboot, when Farhan is not bound, when the user toggles DND on and off, and how Farhan avoids leaving the whole phone silent.

content.text:
**Where the no-text rule came from:** me. I wrote it into the snooze spec as a "privacy" default and never asked you. It was also inconsistent, because Farhan's inbox already stores and shows notification text. I've removed it from the spec and recorded that there is to be no separate Snoozed list. If the red tests contain a guard that enforces the old rule, Sol's implementation pass will drop it. I'll check that in the spec review.

**Silencing the noise:** I think the idea can work, and there's a public Android hook that does roughly this. A notification listener can ask the system to suppress the effects of all notifications while it is connected. What I don't yet know is the detail, so I've started Sol on an emulator test of it. This is my current understanding, still unverified:

- **It's all-or-nothing.** The request covers every notification, not individual ones. Farhan would have to play the sound and vibration itself for everything it lets through. That needs the channel's sound and vibration, which a listener should be able to read for other apps. Heads-up display and the app's channel settings would likely be lost.
- **It shouldn't touch your own Do Not Disturb.** The hint is separate from the interruption filter, so it shouldn't change or leave behind a DND state. The alternatives, changing DND itself or adding an automatic DND rule, would collide with your use of DND, so I'd avoid them. Farhan's own playback would have to follow your DND, ringer mode and volume.
- **The risk is the whole phone going silent.** If Farhan dies while the request is active, it matters whether the system clears it. That's the first thing the test checks, along with reboot and disconnect behaviour.
- **The system's own notification assistant route is probably closed.** I believe third-party apps can't take that role.

I'll report back once it's tested, with a do, don't, or pilot-behind-a-flag recommendation. If it works, the snooze pilot gets simpler: a denied return could be handled silently instead of beeping once.

I'm holding the settings-menu screenshots until your mock-up draft arrives.

Delegated task node:delegated-task:command%3Amcp%3Aa9583e5f-0f51-4b45-be2b-5bf111e74c2e%3Adelegate-task%3A5733023a-40bf-40ab-81e8-d55d3fe81f4f [completed]:
I reviewed the spec, the red tests and the stubs at 938827f. Nothing was edited and nothing was written to git. A test-quality note first: the timing tests use literal UTC instants as their oracle, the policy tests cover every skip reason with no catch-all, and the tests are well annotated. The serious gaps are in the return path and the budget ledger. That is the part the round cares most about, and it has the fewest tests.

File shorthands: **H** = `notification_filter/notification_filter_data/src/test/.../service/SnoozeHandlerTest.kt`, **S** = `research/snooze-pilot-spec.md`, **Svc** = `notification_filter_data/.../service/NotificationService.kt`, **Coord** = `notification_filter_domain/.../delivery/NotificationDeliveryCoordinator.kt`.

## Findings, ranked

**M1 (must). A red test endorses breaking I2.** H:157-162: the second callback at `boundary+30s` must return `true`, and `attempts` must stay at 2. The handler then takes over the post without charging it or snoozing it again, so the notification stays visible and uncharged. That is exactly what I2 (S:67) forbids. A second post of a tracked key inside one boundary means one of two things: the snooze did nothing on Android's side, or the source updated the notification during a race. In both cases it is visible. S:39 ("at most once per boundary") conflicts with I2.
- **Fix:** one rule. A return that Farhan cannot snooze again natively falls through to the proxy path (return `false`, drop the key, log FAILED). The proxy path then queues it under the budget.
- The same rule then covers five more cases: a native retry that throws (M2), the daily bound being hit (S5), `RetryAt` at or before now (S4), no funded moment existing (S6), and a snooze Android never confirms (M6).

**M2 (must). A denied return whose native retry throws has no test and no decision.** The red report defers it (red report :19). Two tests are needed:
- `startSnooze()`, then `rejectSnooze = true`, then a denied return. Expected: `false`, no charges, key dropped, FAILED logged.
- `settleReturn` throwing.
- **Port contract:** `settleReturn` never throws (except cancellation). A store failure after the decision returns `Charged`, with the commit left pending, following the existing `CommitPending` pattern (Coord:269-273). If the handler retried after a write that had already landed, it would charge twice.

**M3 (must). Charge-exactly-once has no tests at the layer that writes the ledger.** `FakeReturnBudget` (H:326-348) is the only budget implementation in the tests. Its retry instant is a literal, so a coordinator that always returns `RetryAt(now + 1h)` would pass every handler test. Missing coordinator tests for `settleSnoozeReturn`:
1. `appendSpend` throws once. Expected: `Charged`; the next gated operation appends exactly one entry; the state is charged once.
2. `write` throws.
3. A denied return performs no `write` and no `appendSpend`.
4. A proxy row with the same id stays undelivered. `finishCompletion` calls `rows.markDelivered(pending.id)` (Coord:114), and row ids are `sbn.key` (Svc:245), so a return with the key of an earlier proxy row would mark that row delivered. `Completion.id` needs to become nullable.
5. The first funded cadence tick is selected, using literal fixtures.
- **Idempotency:** the spend ledger already removes duplicates by `effectId` (`DefaultPreferences.kt:351`). Derive `effectId` from key plus return `postTime` instead of a random UUID. That needs `postTime` added to the `settleReturn` signature (`SnoozeHandler.kt:20-25`).

**M4 (must). E11 contradicts the tests, and the shipped defaults trigger it every night.** E11 (S:92) says a notification should never be snoozed to a tick already known to be unfunded. But `SnoozeInput` has no schedule (`SnoozePolicy.kt:8-26`), and `startSnooze` requires 300 000 ms to 09:00 (H:302-305) even when 09:00 has zero points or no period at all (H:140, H:149).
- **LOW, shipped defaults:** LOW is `ONCE_DAILY`, which ticks only at boundary 0, local midnight (`NotificationDeliveryPolicy.kt:43`). The 00:00-09:00 period has 2 points (`NotificationSchedulePeriod.kt:20`) and LOW costs 8. So every snoozed LOW notification returns at midnight, can make a sound, is denied and is snoozed again.
- **HIGH/MEDIUM, shipped defaults:** the 22:00-24:00 period has 0 points, so anything arriving between 22:00 and 23:00 makes a sound at 23:00.
- **Fix:** one pure function, `nextDeliverableMoment(priority, setting, schedule, budget?, now, zone, testingMode)`: the first cadence tick whose period has at least the priority's point cost. Use it for both the first snooze and `RetryAt`.
- **Owner decision needed:** I7 (S:71) contradicts D5's retry at "next period start" (S:39). Under the defaults no LOW tick is ever funded, so either I7 or the fallback has to give.
- **Unverified aside:** the proxy batch path looks like it can never deliver LOW under the default schedule either (8 points > 2). I haven't checked whether schedule automation changes that.

**M5 (must). Rehydrating from every snoozed key breaks I4 and E14.** `onListenerConnected` rehydrates every key regardless of the toggle (S:39 "whatever the toggle"; H:229-237).
- **Failure:** with snooze never enabled, a notification the user snoozed in SystemUI returns. Farhan charges it, and if the budget is spent, Farhan snoozes it again to a Farhan moment. That overrides the user and breaks I4.
- **E14:** the sentence at S:95 is garbled, and the test charges a key Farhan never saw itself snooze.
- **Missing test:** snooze off, `keysAtConnection = {key}`, return at the boundary. Expected: `false`, `checked` empty.
- **Fix:** a durable ownership record (S1).

**M6 (must). A snooze that does nothing is invisible to the handler.** `snoozeNotification` returns void and can silently do nothing: the 500 limit, a zero or negative delay, or a key that has gone (flexibility doc :7). The handler would log SNOOZED, keep the key and return `true`. The notification stays visible and never passes through the budget, and its stale key later absorbs an update as a "return".
- `FakeSnoozePlatform` (H:353-364) can only throw, so this case cannot be tested today.
- **Fix:** confirm each snooze through the `REASON_SNOOZED` removal within a short window, or fall through to the proxy path. Add `Skip(AT_CAPACITY)` when Farhan's own live count is at or above about 400.

**M7 (must). Returns can be lost from the intake queue.** By design, all returns for a cadence land on the same instant. The intake holds 128 (Svc:75), and on overflow the post is bypassed (Svc:247-252). An overflowed return is visible, uncharged and still tracked.
- Returns while the filter is off (Svc:287 returns early) are also never charged, and their keys go stale.
- **Fix:** check the tracker synchronously in `onNotificationPosted` and put tracked returns in their own pending set. That set is bounded by the 1024-key tracker, so it cannot overflow. Test with 200 simultaneous returns.

**M8 (must). I1 is tested at the wrong layer.** The exclusion flags in `SnoozeInput` default to `false` (`SnoozePolicy.kt:18-25`). A service that forgets to map `FLAG_ONGOING_EVENT` gets an "eligible" input, and Android does not refuse to snooze ongoing, foreground-service, call or alarm notifications (flexibility doc :18).
- **Fix:** remove those defaults. Add a pure mapping from raw `flags` and category to the input, tested with literal constants: 0x2 ongoing, 0x20 no-clear, 0x40 foreground service, 0x200 group summary.

**M9 (must, owner decision). The E12 test is missing, and reboot loss is silent.** S:93 promises "a test that a rehydrated key with no returning post does not leak a counter". No such test exists in any of the four suites.
- The round says nothing may be "silently dropped". E12 together with I3 means a reboot loss leaves no record anywhere.
- I3 is stricter than what the app already does: the proxy path stores title and text in rows (Svc:245-247) and in spend entries. Raise this with the owner.

**S1 (should, architecture). Use the existing `DeliveryRowStore` as the durable ledger.** It would replace the in-memory tracker and rehydration. One row per snoozed key holds state SNOOZED, the priority at snooze time and the deadline. That gives:
- ownership, which fixes M5;
- loss detection: deadline passed and the key in neither the active nor the snoozed list means LOST. It shows in the inbox and can be delivered from the row (M9);
- returns that happened while Farhan was disconnected can be charged when it reconnects;
- stale-key cleanup;
- the row change and the budget write in one completion, which helps M3.

This requires the owner to change I3. If they refuse, persist a salted hash of the key with its deadline and priority.

**S2 (should). D6 and H:258-271 contradict the research.** The flexibility doc (§4 :73) says a source cancelling a hidden record produces no per-item removal callback. Stale keys therefore build up, and edge 4 (S:56) becomes common rather than rare. The test is still valid as a race case. Fix: store a deadline per key and drop the key at deadline plus a grace period.

**S3 (should). Each return counts as a new arrival.** Returns go through classification again, which calls `rateTracker.record` (Svc:360). If 15 messages from one app return at 09:00, they can trip the flood threshold. The degraded priority costs more points (HIGH 2 → LOW 8), so more returns are denied, and the app's genuinely new posts get demoted. Fix: charge a return at the priority recorded at snooze time, and do not record it in the rate window.

**S4 (should). `RetryAt` can already be in the past.** The handler computes `retryAt - input.now`. When the queue is backed up, that can be zero or negative, which Android silently ignores. Also, `settleReturn(at)` and the coordinator's `environment.timeContext()` are two different clocks: keep one. Test: `retryAt = boundary` should fall through to the proxy path or settle again.

**S5 (should). The per-key daily bound has no number and no test** (S:62). With M4's targeting, one denial per period is the natural limit. Set a cap (for example 3 a day), fall through to the proxy path when it is hit, and test 4 denials.

**S6 (should). Nothing handles "no funded moment exists"** (all periods 0, or every period's budget below the point cost). `RetryAt` cannot express it. Bound the search (for example 48 h), add a third outcome, and fall through to the proxy path.

**S7 (should). Groups are an unverified loss path.** Snoozing an only child also snoozes its summary (flexibility doc :18). I am not certain whether the proxy path's `cancelNotification` on a summary (Svc:310) reaches hidden children through AOSP's group-cancel logic. Add device evidence (f): one eligible child plus its summary, and confirm the child returns. Until that passes, the pilot can skip any notification with a group key.

**S8 (should). The rehydrate test would pass a wrong implementation.** H:229-237 reuses the same handler instance, and `snoozedKeys()` never changes. A handler that skips `onListenerConnected` and checks `snoozedKeys()` on every post passes the test. In production that fails, because the key has left the snoozed list by the time it returns. Fix: the fake removes returned keys from the snoozed list, and the test builds a second `SnoozeHandler`.

**N1 (nit).** H:77-78 assert the fake's own arithmetic. They can only fail if `settleReturn` is called a different number of times, which H:76 already checks.

**N2 (nit).** Small spec inconsistencies:
- D8 (S:42) says "no key in memory", but D5's tracker keeps keys in memory.
- Evidence item (a) (S:78) still says "chosen duration", left over from v1.
- D2 (S:36) writes CRITICAL as `Skip(IMMEDIATE_CADENCE)`, but the code has `Skip(CRITICAL)`.

**N3 (nit).** `SnoozeTiming.delayUntilNextMoment` takes `priority` and never uses it. An IMMEDIATELY cadence can be passed in; a batch-only cadence type would make that impossible.

**N4 (nit).** Missing tracker test: recording an existing key again must make it the newest. Otherwise a key that was snoozed again can be evicted first.

## Answers to the five questions

1. **Gaps in states and lifecycle:**
   - Reboot: M9.
   - Android sounds before Farhan decides: M4. The shipped defaults make this happen nightly for LOW.
   - Ownership after rehydration: M5 and S1.
   - 500 limit: M6.
   - Groups: S7.
   - Also: queue overflow (M7), returns while disconnected (S1), and double-counted arrivals (S3).
2. **Contradictions:**
   - D5 with I2 and H:160 (M1).
   - E11 with H:140/149/302 (M4).
   - I7 with D5's retry (M4).
   - E14 and I4 with D5 and H:229 (M5).
   - D6 with the research (S2).
   - D8 with D5 (N2).
3. **Hollow red tests:**
   - H:160 asserts a violation of I2.
   - H:229-237 passes with lazy rehydration.
   - `FakeReturnBudget`'s literal `RetryAt` hides any coordinator selection bug.
   - H:77-78 test the fake.
   - The policy suite is sound, but at the wrong layer for I1 (M8).
   - The timing suite is good: literal instants are the oracle, and the production checks are a supplement.
4. **Missing tests:** partial write (M3), per-key daily bound (S5), retry that throws (M2), a snooze that does nothing (M6), queue overflow (M7), the E12 counter (M9), and snooze off with foreign snoozed keys (M5).
5. **Simpler designs and reuse:**
   - The coordinator under `DeliveryGate`, with a nullable-id `Completion` and a deterministic `effectId`.
   - One `nextDeliverableMoment`, built on `DeliveryTimeContext.from` and `isBatchTickForCadence`, for both the first snooze and the retry.
   - The proxy path as the single fallback (M1).
   - `DeliveryRowStore` as the ownership ledger (S1).

SCORE[error-paths]: 4/10
SCORE[durability]: 3/10
SCORE[architecture]: 6/10
SCORE[legibility]: 6/10

Take a look at Clear SMS. It is an app that I have starred on GitHub. It has a filtering system that I would like to leverage. Please take a look at the open issues, particularly those that I have commented on. And then let's leverage the filtering work that they have to make this app have a filtering system that allows us to have different sorts of running balances and items that can be extracted from each of our notifications. Then with those details, we can do things like make charts, add status indicators, so forth... none of the mock-ups really tickle my fancy the forecast one looks kind of alright, but it isn't the sort of design language that I was thinking of. I was thinking of something that's more intrinsic to the notifications themselves, rather than what the app itself is doing. 4. M6 (confirm each snooze via the REASON_SNOOZED callback within a window). The callback is the only confirmation, but the window is a timer, i.e. new state. What happens on a slow device where the callback arrives after the window? Is `Skip(AT_CAPACITY)` at 400 plus treating an unconfirmed snooze as 'return later, fall through to proxy' enough without the timer?

I accept M1, M2, M3, M5, M8, S2-S6, N1-N4 as written.

I've started the ClearSMS research, which will cover the filtering system and your design direction. It isn't finished yet.

**What I found so far, from GitHub only (I haven't commented or posted anything there):**
- ClearSMS is Apache-2.0, in Kotlin, and describes itself as offline. It "extracts transactions into a personal finance dashboard", sorts messages into categories, and handles one-time codes and bill reminders.
- Your own activity there is issue #5, "Missing Critical Features", which you filed. I found no other comments from you.
- The issues that matter most for you are the finance ones. They show where its extraction goes wrong, which is what we want to avoid copying:
  - **#9, "Finance Balance":** the big headline balance sums every account, and the reporter wants only selected accounts counted.
  - **#155:** use the balance printed in the message instead of a running sum.
  - **#166:** a transaction was missed or wrongly classified, even after the reporter made a rule from the message.
  - **#165, #170:** add a note to a transaction; classify SIP investments.

Filed, and I've added it to the ClearSMS research that's already running. It now has a section on one-time codes (OTPs).

**What the researcher will cover:**
- How ClearSMS spots a code and what it does with it: copy, hide, expiry, and its own OTP issues.
- How that fits Farhan's per-app and per-category settings, with the code as one more thing extracted from a notification. A code should probably never wait behind the budget, and I'll ask for a recommendation on that.
- Whether Farhan can see the code at all, which is the main risk. Android 15 hides one-time codes from notification content for apps that are only listening, and Farhan is one of those. ClearSMS avoids this because it is the SMS app and reads the messages directly. I'll know which Android versions are affected, what you can switch on, and what the options are if Farhan can't see the code. They may include a companion-device association or the SMS permission route.

I'll bring back what Android allows and a recommendation. This may turn out to be a feature that works only for some apps or some Android versions, and I'll say so plainly if it does.

Short answers, all from code. Nothing edited.

## 1. S1 after I3 is removed: yes, reuse the row store

**Smallest record that fixes M5 and M9.** Per snoozed key: the deadline, the priority at snooze time, and the boot count at snooze time.
- Deadline fixes M5 (ownership) and S2 (stale keys).
- Priority is what S3 needs.
- Boot count (`Settings.Global.BOOT_COUNT`) fixes M9. Without it, Farhan can't tell a reboot loss from a source cancelling while snoozed: in both cases the key is neither active nor snoozed after the deadline.

The smallest place to keep that is a capped JSON list in preferences, like the spend ledger (`DefaultPreferences.kt:349-358`). It needs no migration.

**Why the row store still wins.**
- **Inbox parity.** Today every filtered notification gets an inbox row at arrival (the upsert in `onArrival`, Coord:165-171), and the inbox shows every row that isn't cleared (`NotificationQueries.kt:6`). If snooze keeps only a side ledger, snoozed notifications disappear from Farhan's inbox. That's a regression against the proxy path. It isn't a new Snoozed list: it's the same inbox row the proxy path already writes, and yes, showing it is wanted.
- **Lost items get delivered for free.** A row lost to a reboot becomes an ordinary pending row (clear its deadline), and the existing batch path proxy-delivers it under the budget. A side ledger can only say "lost".
- **One commit.** The return's `Completion` marks the row delivered and writes the budget under the same gate. That's what M3 needs.

**Cost.**
- One nullable column (`snoozeDeadline`) and a Room migration.
- That column must go into the WHERE of all three pending queries (`NotificationDao.kt:16`, `:18`, `:77`). Otherwise `onBatchTick` proxies a row while Android still holds the original, and you get a duplicate. `onBatchTick`'s visible-source deferral (Coord:232) doesn't protect against this, because a hidden record isn't active.

**Key collision.** Rows are keyed by `sbn.key` on purpose. The proxy path already treats a later post with the same key as the same notification: the upsert replaces the row. With S1 the snooze is that same upsert, so any pending proxy row with that key becomes the snoozed row, exactly as a source update would replace it today. The return then marks its own row delivered.

The M3.4 hazard only exists in the stub design, where a return owns no row and `markDelivered(key)` touches someone else's. One edge remains: the post updates a row that was already proxy-delivered. The existing refresh branch handles that today (Coord:176), so the snooze policy should skip it, with a reason like `ALREADY_DELIVERED`.

## 2. Keep I7, fall back to the proxy path: agreed, with one correction

Nothing gets stuck that isn't already stuck today, provided three conditions hold:

- **"Funded" is a static test.** A tick is funded when it falls in a period with points ≥ the priority's point cost, or the priority's setting is IGNORING. Spend and the hourly cap at that tick are decided at return. If the return is denied, the notification is snoozed again to the next funded tick, bounded by S5's daily cap, then the proxy path.
- **The search must use each date's own schedule (the correction).** `environment.schedule()` is today's schedule only (`DefaultPreferences.kt:246-247`, `scheduleFor(today)`). A 48 h search has to call `ScheduleBook.scheduleAt(tick, zone)` for every tick. If it doesn't, a dated override tomorrow is misjudged: either the notification is snoozed into an unfunded period (a sound on denial), or it falls back when it didn't need to. `DeliveryEnvironment` needs the schedule book or a `scheduleAt(instant)`.
- **The horizon in testing mode** is 960 three-minute boundaries. `ONCE_DAILY` still ticks only at boundary 0, so LOW has the same two candidates as in production.

**LOW on the proxy path is an existing bug, but not on `main`.** `main` has no `NotificationDeliveryPolicy` at all (`git ls-tree main` finds 0 matches). The bug lives on the pilot base: neither file changed since 717faf6. Nothing rescues it:
- `onBatchTick` offers only rows that pass `shouldDeliverOnBatchTick` (Coord:218-220). For LOW that's boundary 0 only (`NotificationDeliveryPolicy.kt:43`).
- At midnight, `canDeliverNow` finds the 2-point period and the cost of 8, so the row is deferred, every day.
- The "standing" degradation is inbox display only (`NotificationQueries.kt:7,33`, `NotificationInboxFilter.kt:17`). There's no carry-over or escalation.
- `NotificationDeliveryPolicyTest.kt:118` tests LOW's cadence on its own and never together with `DEFAULT_SCHEDULE`.

Under the default schedule, LOW is never pushed: it only ever shows in the inbox. So falling back to the proxy path matches today's behaviour. It isn't lost, but the owner should hear it as a separate bug.

## 3. Against the one-minute re-snooze

- **It breaks I7**, because one minute later isn't a cadence tick.
- **It doesn't converge.** Every overflowed return has already made its sound (E11). Snoozing them all for one minute brings them back at one instant, so the burst repeats, possibly with a sound every minute. The 128-item intake drains slowly, because each item is classified and does I/O.
- **Raising the bound is expensive.** Each queued item can carry up to 1 024 chars of title, 16 384 chars of text and 8 actions with their intents (Svc:245-251). A return needs only its key and `postTime` once S3 (charge at the priority recorded at snooze) is accepted.

**Simpler than both:** the "pending set" is just a field on the entry you already have. `onNotificationPosted` already has to check the tracker synchronously. When it finds the key, it sets `returnedAt = postTime` on that entry and offers a small `Work.Return(key)`. If the offer fails, the flag stays set, and the worker settles flagged entries on its next item or at the next batch tick. No new structure, no loss on overflow, and the bound is the tracker's own.

## 4. No timer: decide from Android's state, not from elapsed time

**A late callback after a timer causes a duplicate.** The timer expires and Farhan falls through to the proxy path. Its `cancelNotification` on the now-hidden key does nothing (flexibility doc §4:73, verified on device). Farhan queues and delivers a proxy, then the original returns at its deadline. That's a duplicate, and it's charged twice. So a timer is wrong.

**`Skip(AT_CAPACITY)` alone isn't enough.** It counts only Farhan's own snoozes. Android's limit of 500 includes the user's and other listeners' snoozes, and zero-delay or missing-key snoozes also do nothing. Keep it, and add a check against Android's own state:

- **Rule:** an entry snoozed before the previous batch tick, never confirmed, and still in `getActiveNotifications()` with the same `postTime` did not snooze. Hand it to the proxy path.
- **Where it runs:** at the next batch tick, which already reads `activeSourceKeys()` (Coord:217), and at connect.
- **Why it's safe on a slow device:** a snooze that landed late is not in the active list, so it can't produce a duplicate. The "before the previous tick" condition orders the check against existing events (an hour, or 3 minutes in testing mode). Requiring one full tick also avoids a race where the next tick fires seconds after the snooze call.
- **What `REASON_SNOOZED` does:** it only marks the entry confirmed early.
- **Cost:** a notification that never actually snoozed bypasses the budget for at most about two ticks.
- **A second post of the same key while unconfirmed:** handle it with M1's rule (fall through to the proxy path). A key that really is hidden doesn't produce a callback when the source updates it (E13).

The scores and verdict stand, with one change: with S1 unblocked, architecture moves to 7/10. VERDICT: CHANGES.

The 00:00-09:00 period has 2 points (`NotificationSchedulePeriod.kt:20`) and LOW costs 8. So every snoozed LOW notification returns at midnight, can make a sound, is denied and is snoozed again.
- **HIGH/MEDIUM, shipped defaults:** the 22:00-24:00 period has 0 points, so anything arriving between 22:00 and 23:00 makes a sound at 23:00.
- **Fix:** one pure function, `nextDeliverableMoment(priority, setting, schedule, budget?, now, zone, testingMode)`: the first cadence tick whose period has at least the priority's point cost. Use it for both the first snooze and `RetryAt`.
- **Owner decision needed:** I7 (S:71) contradicts D5's retry at "next period start" (S:39). Under the defaults no LOW tick is ever funded, so either I7 or the fallback has to give.
- **Unverified aside:** the proxy batch path looks like it can never deliver LOW under the default schedule either (8 points > 2). I haven't checked whether schedule automation changes that.

**M5 (must). Rehydrating from every snoozed key breaks I4 and E14.** `onListenerConnected` rehydrates every key regardless of the toggle (S:39 "whatever the toggle"; H:229-237).
- **Failure:** with snooze never enabled, a notification the user snoozed in SystemUI returns. Farhan charges it, and if the budget is spent, Farhan snoozes it again to a Farhan moment. That overrides the user and breaks I4.
- **E14:** the sentence at S:95 is garbled, and the test charges a key Farhan never saw itself snooze.
- **Missing test:** snooze off, `keysAtConnection = {key}`, return at the boundary. Expected: `false`, `checked` empty.
- **Fix:** a durable ownership record (S1).

**M6 (must). A snooze that does nothing is invisible to the handler.** `snoozeNotification` returns void and can silently do nothing: the 500 limit, a zero or negative delay, or a key that has gone (flexibility doc :7). The handler would log SNOOZED, keep the key and return `true`. The notification stays visible and never passes through the budget, and its stale key later absorbs an update as a "return".
- `FakeSnoozePlatform` (H:353-364) can only throw, so this case cannot be tested today.
- **Fix:** confirm each snooze through the `REASON_SNOOZED` removal within a short window, or fall through to the proxy path. Add `Skip(AT_CAPACITY)` when Farhan's own live count is at or above about 400.

**M7 (must). Returns can be lost from the intake queue.** By design, all returns for a cadence land on the same instant. The intake holds 128 (Svc:75), and on overflow the post is bypassed (Svc:247-252). An overflowed return is visible, uncharged and still tracked.
- Returns while the filter is off (Svc:287 returns early) are also never charged, and their keys go stale.
- **Fix:** check the tracker synchronously in `onNotificationPosted` and put tracked returns in their own pending set. That set is bounded by the 1024-key tracker, so it cannot overflow. Test with 200 simultaneous returns.

**M8 (must). I1 is tested at the wrong layer.** The exclusion flags in `SnoozeInput` default to `false` (`SnoozePolicy.kt:18-25`). A service that forgets to map `FLAG_ONGOING_EVENT` gets an "eligible" input, and Android does not refuse to snooze ongoing, foreground-service, call or alarm notifications (flexibility doc :18).
- **Fix:** remove those defaults. Add a pure mapping from raw `flags` and category to the input, tested with literal constants: 0x2 ongoing, 0x20 no-clear, 0x40 foreground service, 0x200 group summary.

**M9 (must, owner decision). The E12 test is missing, and reboot loss is silent.** S:93 promises "a test that a rehydrated key with no returning post does not leak a counter". No such test exists in any of the four suites.
- The round says nothing may be "silently dropped". E12 together with I3 means a reboot loss leaves no record anywhere.
- I3 is stricter than what the app already does: the proxy path stores title and text in rows (Svc:245-247) and in spend entries. Raise this with the owner.

**S1 (should, architecture). Use the existing `DeliveryRowStore` as the durable ledger.** It would replace the in-memory tracker and rehydration. One row per snoozed key holds state SNOOZED, the priority at snooze time and the deadline. That gives:
- ownership, which fixes M5;
- loss detection: deadline passed and the key in neither the active nor the snoozed list means LOST. It shows in the inbox and can be delivered from the row (M9);
- returns that happened while Farhan was disconnected can be charged when it reconnects;
- stale-key cleanup;
- the row change and the budget write in one completion, which helps M3.

This requires the owner to change I3. If they refuse, persist a salted hash of the key with its deadline and priority.

**S2 (should). D6 and H:258-271 contradict the research.** The flexibility doc (§4 :73) says a source cancelling a hidden record produces no per-item removal callback. Stale keys therefore build up, and edge 4 (S:56) becomes common rather than rare. The test is still valid as a race case. Fix: store a deadline per key and drop the key at deadline plus a grace period.

**S3 (should). Each return counts as a new arrival.** Returns go through classification again, which calls `rateTracker.record` (Svc:360). If 15 messages from one app return at 09:00, they can trip the flood threshold. The degraded priority costs more points (HIGH 2 → LOW 8), so more returns are denied, and the app's genuinely new posts get demoted. Fix: charge a return at the priority recorded at snooze time, and do not record it in the rate window.

**S4 (should). `RetryAt` can already be in the past.** The handler computes `retryAt - input.now`. When the queue is backed up, that can be zero or negative, which Android silently ignores. Also, `settleReturn(at)` and the coordinator's `environment.timeContext()` are two different clocks: keep one. Test: `retryAt = boundary` should fall through to the proxy path or settle again.

**S5 (should). The per-key daily bound has no number and no test** (S:62). With M4's targeting, one denial per period is the natural limit. Set a cap (for example 3 a day), fall through to the proxy path when it is hit, and test 4 denials.

**S6 (should). Nothing handles "no funded moment exists"** (all periods 0, or every period's budget below the point cost). `RetryAt` cannot express it. Bound the search (for example 48 h), add a third outcome, and fall through to the proxy path.

**S7 (should). Groups are an unverified loss path.** Snoozing an only child also snoozes its summary (flexibility doc :18). I am not certain whether the proxy path's `cancelNotification` on a summary (Svc:310) reaches hidden children through AOSP's group-cancel logic. Add device evidence (f): one eligible child plus its summary, and confirm the child returns. Until that passes, the pilot can skip any notification with a group key.

**S8 (should). The rehydrate test would pass a wrong implementation.** H:229-237 reuses the same handler instance, and `snoozedKeys()` never changes. A handler that skips `onListenerConnected` and checks `snoozedKeys()` on every post passes the test. In production that fails, because the key has left the snoozed list by the time it returns. Fix: the fake removes returned keys from the snoozed list, and the test builds a second `SnoozeHandler`.

**N1 (nit).** H:77-78 assert the fake's own arithmetic. They can only fail if `settleReturn` is called a different number of times, which H:76 already checks.

**N2 (nit).** Small spec inconsistencies:
- D8 (S:42) says "no key in memory", but D5's tracker keeps keys in memory.
- Evidence item (a) (S:78) still says "chosen duration", left over from v1.
- D2 (S:36) writes CRITICAL as `Skip(IMMEDIATE_CADENCE)`, but the code has `Skip(CRITICAL)`.

**N3 (nit).** `SnoozeTiming.delayUntilNextMoment` takes `priority` and never uses it. An IMMEDIATELY cadence can be passed in; a batch-only cadence type would make that impossible.

**N4 (nit).** Missing tracker test: recording an existing key again must make it the newest. Otherwise a key that was snoozed again can be evicted first.

## Answers to the five questions

1. **Gaps in states and lifecycle:**
   - Reboot: M9.
   - Android sounds before Farhan decides: M4. The shipped defaults make this happen nightly for LOW.
   - Ownership after rehydration: M5 and S1.
   - 500 limit: M6.
   - Groups: S7.
   - Also: queue overflow (M7), returns while disconnected (S1), and double-counted arrivals (S3).
2. **Contradictions:**
   - D5 with I2 and H:160 (M1).
   - E11 with H:140/149/302 (M4).
   - I7 with D5's retry (M4).
   - E14 and I4 with D5 and H:229 (M5).
   - D6 with the research (S2).
   - D8 with D5 (N2).
3. **Hollow red tests:**
   - H:160 asserts a violation of I2.
   - H:229-237 passes with lazy rehydration.
   - `FakeReturnBudget`'s literal `RetryAt` hides any coordinator selection bug.
   - H:77-78 test the fake.
   - The policy suite is sound, but at the wrong layer for I1 (M8).
   - The timing suite is good: literal instants are the oracle, and the production checks are a supplement.
4. **Missing tests:** partial write (M3), per-key daily bound (S5), retry that throws (M2), a snooze that does nothing (M6), queue overflow (M7), the E12 counter (M9), and snooze off with foreign snoozed keys (M5).
5. **Simpler designs and reuse:**
   - The coordinator under `DeliveryGate`, with a nullable-id `Completion` and a deterministic `effectId`.
   - One `nextDeliverableMoment`, built on `DeliveryTimeContext.from` and `isBatchTickForCadence`, for both the first snooze and the retry.
   - The proxy path as the single fallback (M1).
   - `DeliveryRowStore` as the ownership ledger (S1).

SCORE[error-paths]: 4/10
SCORE[durability]: 3/10
SCORE[architecture]: 6/10
SCORE[legibility]: 6/10

## 1. S1 after I3 is removed: yes, reuse the row store

**Smallest record that fixes M5 and M9.** Per snoozed key: the deadline, the priority at snooze time, and the boot count at snooze time.
- Deadline fixes M5 (ownership) and S2 (stale keys).
- Priority is what S3 needs.
- Boot count (`Settings.Global.BOOT_COUNT`) fixes M9. Without it, Farhan can't tell a reboot loss from a source cancelling while snoozed: in both cases the key is neither active nor snoozed after the deadline.

The smallest place to keep that is a capped JSON list in preferences, like the spend ledger (`DefaultPreferences.kt:349-358`). It needs no migration.

**Why the row store still wins.**
- **Inbox parity.** Today every filtered notification gets an inbox row at arrival (the upsert in `onArrival`, Coord:165-171), and the inbox shows every row that isn't cleared (`NotificationQueries.kt:6`). If snooze keeps only a side ledger, snoozed notifications disappear from Farhan's inbox. That's a regression against the proxy path. It isn't a new Snoozed list: it's the same inbox row the proxy path already writes, and yes, showing it is wanted.
- **Lost items get delivered for free.** A row lost to a reboot becomes an ordinary pending row (clear its deadline), and the existing batch path proxy-delivers it under the budget. A side ledger can only say "lost".
- **One commit.** The return's `Completion` marks the row delivered and writes the budget under the same gate. That's what M3 needs.

**Cost.**
- One nullable column (`snoozeDeadline`) and a Room migration.
- That column must go into the WHERE of all three pending queries (`NotificationDao.kt:16`, `:18`, `:77`). Otherwise `onBatchTick` proxies a row while Android still holds the original, and you get a duplicate. `onBatchTick`'s visible-source deferral (Coord:232) doesn't protect against this, because a hidden record isn't active.

**Key collision.** Rows are keyed by `sbn.key` on purpose. The proxy path already treats a later post with the same key as the same notification: the upsert replaces the row. With S1 the snooze is that same upsert, so any pending proxy row with that key becomes the snoozed row, exactly as a source update would replace it today. The return then marks its own row delivered.

The M3.4 hazard only exists in the stub design, where a return owns no row and `markDelivered(key)` touches someone else's. One edge remains: the post updates a row that was already proxy-delivered. The existing refresh branch handles that today (Coord:176), so the snooze policy should skip it, with a reason like `ALREADY_DELIVERED`.

## 2. Keep I7, fall back to the proxy path: agreed, with one correction

Nothing gets stuck that isn't already stuck today, provided three conditions hold:

- **"Funded" is a static test.** A tick is funded when it falls in a period with points ≥ the priority's point cost, or the priority's setting is IGNORING. Spend and the hourly cap at that tick are decided at return. If the return is denied, the notification is snoozed again to the next funded tick, bounded by S5's daily cap, then the proxy path.
- **The search must use each date's own schedule (the correction).** `environment.schedule()` is today's schedule only (`DefaultPreferences.kt:246-247`, `scheduleFor(today)`). A 48 h search has to call `ScheduleBook.scheduleAt(tick, zone)` for every tick. If it doesn't, a dated override tomorrow is misjudged: either the notification is snoozed into an unfunded period (a sound on denial), or it falls back when it didn't need to. `DeliveryEnvironment` needs the schedule book or a `scheduleAt(instant)`.
- **The horizon in testing mode** is 960 three-minute boundaries. `ONCE_DAILY` still ticks only at boundary 0, so LOW has the same two candidates as in production.

**LOW on the proxy path is an existing bug, but not on `main`.** `main` has no `NotificationDeliveryPolicy` at all (`git ls-tree main` finds 0 matches). The bug lives on the pilot base: neither file changed since 717faf6. Nothing rescues it:
